title: The Tinderbox
summary: A soldier came marching along the high road with his knapsack on his back and a sword at his side: left, right, left, right! He had been to the wars and was now returning home with...
full_text:
A soldier came marching along the high road with his knapsack on his back and a sword at his side: left, right, left, right! He had been to the wars and was now returning home with cheerful spirits, though his pockets were completely empty.

On the edge of the dark forest, he met an old witch. "Good evening, brave soldier!" croaked the witch. "How would you like to have as much gold and silver as your heart desires?"

The soldier halted and listened. The witch pointed to a giant hollow oak tree. "Climb to the top, and you will find an opening. Tie this rope around your waist, and I will lower you into the earth. At the bottom runs a great hall illuminated by three hundred burning lamps. You will pass three doors. Behind the first door sits a great chest guarded by a dog with eyes as large as teacups. Place my blue checked apron upon the floor, set the dog upon it, and take as many copper coppers as you please! Behind the second door sits a dog with eyes as large as mill-wheels; place him upon the apron, and take as much shining silver as you can carry! Behind the third door sits a monster of a dog with eyes as large as round towers; set him upon the apron, and you may fill your pockets with pure gold! In return, bring me only the old tinderbox my grandmother left behind."

The soldier boldly climbed the oak, descended into the hall, and filled his pockets, his boots, and his knapsack with gleaming gold from the third chest. Then he grabbed the old tinderbox and called out to be pulled up. When the witch refused to tell him why she desired the tinderbox above all the gold, a quarrel arose, and the soldier hurried away into the grand royal city.

Now wealthy, the soldier lived in splendor, bought fine clothes, and gave generously to the poor. But soon his gold was spent, and he moved to a dingy garret. In the darkness of the evening, remembering the tinderbox, he struck it once. Sparks flew, and instantly the dog with eyes as large as teacups appeared, barking: "What is my lord's command?"

"Bring me some money!" said the soldier. The dog darted off and returned with a heavy bag of copper. When he struck the box twice, the dog of silver appeared; when he struck it three times, the giant dog of gold arrived!

The soldier learned of the beautiful princess kept locked inside a copper castle because of a prophecy that she would marry a common soldier. Yearning to see her, he struck the box. The great dog brought the sleeping princess on its back through the midnight air. The soldier kissed her hand with tender reverence, and the dog carried her back safely.

When the queen discovered the visits by tying a bag of buckwheat with a small hole to the princess's waist, the soldier was arrested and sentenced to the gallows. But on the scaffold, the soldier asked one last wish: to smoke a final pipe of tobacco. He drew his tinderbox and struck it: once, twice, thrice!

All three enormous dogs leaped into the square, tossing the unjust judges and cruel guards into the air. The townsfolk cheered, rejoicing that an honest, generous soldier would be their king. The princess was released from her copper prison, and they were married amid seven days of joyous festivities, with the three marvelous dogs sitting at the royal banquet table, their huge eyes shining with delight.
moral: True fortune favors courage and presence of mind, but generosity toward others is what preserves genuine happiness.

title: Little Claus and Big Claus
summary: In a certain village lived two men who bore the very same name: Claus. One owned four strong horses and was called Big Claus; the other owned only a single humble horse and was cal...
full_text:
In a certain village lived two men who bore the very same name: Claus. One owned four strong horses and was called Big Claus; the other owned only a single humble horse and was called Little Claus.

Every weekday, Little Claus plowed the fields for Big Claus with his one horse. On Sundays, Big Claus loaned his four horses to Little Claus so he could plow his own small plot. Little Claus was so proud that as the village churchgoers passed by, he would crack his whip and cry out: "Gee up, all my five horses!"

"You must not say that!" snarled Big Claus. "Only one of those horses belongs to you!" But when the next crowd passed, Little Claus forgot himself and shouted once more: "Gee up, all my horses!" In a fit of petty rage, Big Claus seized a mallet and struck Little Claus's only horse dead.

Little Claus wept, but he did not despair. He skinned the horse, dried the hide thoroughly, placed it in a sack, and walked toward the town to sell the leather. Caught in a storm, he sought shelter at a farmhouse. Through the window, he saw the farmer's wife entertaining the village parish clerk with roast meat, wine, and sweet cakes. When the suspicious husband returned, the wife hid the feast in the oven and concealed the clerk inside a large wooden chest.

The farmer welcomed Little Claus and offered him plain gruel. Under the table, Little Claus stepped on his dried horsehide, making it squeak loudly. "What has your sack got to say?" asked the curious farmer.

"My sack is a wizard," whispered Little Claus. "He says he has conjured roast meat and wine into your baking oven!" The farmer opened the oven, found the delicious feast, and ate in astonishment. When the sack squeaked again, Little Claus declared that the wizard had conjured the parish clerk into the chest. The farmer was so amazed by the magical sack that he gave Little Claus a bushel of silver coins and the heavy wooden chest to take away.

Out on the road near a deep bridge, Little Claus pretended he was going to heave the heavy chest into the river. The clerk terrified within shouted: "Spare me, and I will give you another full bushel of silver!" Little Claus took the coins and let the clerk go free.

When Big Claus saw Little Claus returning with two full bushels of silver, his eyes bulged with envy. "Where did you get so much treasure?" he demanded.

"I sold the hide of my horse in town," said Little Claus calmly.

Big Claus rushed home, slaughtered all four of his fine horses, and hauled their skins to the city, demanding a bushel of silver for each. The tanners laughed at him and drove him away with sticks. Realizing he had been outwitted, Big Claus stormed back, determined on revenge, but Little Claus's quick wit and cool head continually turned the bully's own traps against him until Big Claus was washed away by his own reckless greed, leaving Little Claus to live in peace and prosperity with his newfound fortune.
moral: Greed and bullying ultimately bring their own downfall, while quiet wit and patience overcome brutal force.

title: The Princess and the Pea
summary: Once upon a time, there was a young prince who longed to marry a princess; but she must be a real princess—one possessing true nobility of soul, grace, and exquisite refinement. He...
full_text:
Once upon a time, there was a young prince who longed to marry a princess; but she must be a real princess—one possessing true nobility of soul, grace, and exquisite refinement. He traveled across the four corners of the world in search of his ideal, but everywhere he met disappointment. There were princesses in abundance, but whether they were genuine in character was impossible to ascertain; there was always something in their conduct or manners that felt artificial. So the prince returned home to his father's palace, sorrowful and heavy of heart.

One dark evening, a terrible tempest raged over the land. Thunder crashed in deafening bursts, lightning tore open the black sky, and the rain poured down in torrents. It was a fearful night.

Suddenly, a knock was heard at the town gate, and the old king went himself to open it.

Standing outside in the gale was a young maiden. Merciful heavens, what a sight the storm had made of her! Water streamed down from her hair and soaked through her torn garments; it ran in at the tips of her shoes and flowed out at the heels. Yet she stood with calm dignity and declared that she was a real princess.

"Well, we shall soon find out the truth of that!" thought the old queen mother. But she said not a single word. She went quietly into the guest chamber, stripped all the bedding from the royal bedstead, and placed a single tiny green garden pea directly upon the bare wooden boards. Then she laid twenty thick mattresses over the pea, and piled twenty down comforters stuffed with soft eiderdown upon the mattresses.

On this towering couch, the storm-tossed maiden was invited to rest for the night.

In the morning, the royal family gathered at the breakfast table. The queen asked the princess kindly: "Did you sleep well, my dear?"

"Oh, miserably!" replied the maiden softly. "I scarcely closed my eyes the entire night. Heaven alone knows what was in the bed! I lay upon something so terribly hard that my whole body is bruised black and blue. It was dreadful!"

Now they knew with certainty that she was a real princess! No one but a true princess could have possessed a delicacy so refined as to feel a tiny pea through twenty thick mattresses and twenty eiderdown comforters.

The prince took her for his beloved bride with boundless joy, knowing he had found his genuine princess. And the pea was placed in the royal cabinet of curiosities, where it may still be seen to this day, unless someone has carried it away. And that is a true story!
moral: True nobility of spirit cannot be disguised; genuine gentleness and sensitivity shine through every circumstance.

title: Little Ida's Flowers
summary: "My poor flowers are quite dead!" sighed little Ida, gazing sorrowfully at her bouquet of withered blossoms on the parlor table. "Yesterday evening they were so fresh and radiant,...
full_text:
"My poor flowers are quite dead!" sighed little Ida, gazing sorrowfully at her bouquet of withered blossoms on the parlor table. "Yesterday evening they were so fresh and radiant, and now their leaves are drooping! Why do they fade so quickly?"

A cheerful young student sitting by the window looked up from cutting paper silhouettes. "Do you not know what they did last night?" he smiled. "The flowers went to the grand midnight ball! That is why they hang their heads today in sweet exhaustion."

"Do flowers dance?" asked Ida, her wide blue eyes sparkling with wonder.

"Certainly!" answered the student. "As soon as darkness falls and we mortals go to sleep, the flowers leap merrily from their pots and vases. They dance across the polished floor of the king's castle, where the white lilies play the harp, the yellow buttercups beat the drums, and the roses wear golden crowns. The blue violets are young naval cadets who waltz with hyacinths and daisies!"

An old, stern privy councilor in the corner grunted: "What nonsense to put into a child's head—mere wild imagination!"

But little Ida believed every word of the student's enchanting tale. That night, she gently took her sick flowers, laid them carefully in her doll Sophie's warm canopied bed, and whispered: "Rest well, little flowers; you shall sleep peacefully tonight."

In the middle of the night, Ida awoke to the soft chime of music coming from the drawing room. Tiptoeing to the doorway, she peered through the crack. Moonlight flooded the floor, and lo! All the flowers in the house were holding a magnificent festival! The tall yellow lily stood at the piano, playing lively dance tunes; tulips and daffodils bowed to one another in graceful quadrilles; and the withered bouquet in the doll's bed had risen to dance with joyous vitality across the rug! Even the wooden nutcracker and the old brass tongs hopped about in merry rhythm.

In the morning, little Ida ran to the bed and found her flowers once more quiet, dry, and withered. But she was not sad. She wrapped them tenderly in a silk handkerchief, carried them out into the bright garden sunshine, and buried them beneath the green turf alongside her cousin. "Sleep sweetly through the cold winter, dear flowers," whispered Ida with a smile, "for I know that when the warm spring returns, you will rise again from the earth, more radiant and beautiful than ever before."
moral: The innocence of childhood finds living beauty and empathy in every corner of the natural world.

title: Thumbelina
summary: Once upon a time, a lonely woman who longed for a little child sought counsel from a wise old woman. The old woman gave her a magic barleycorn, saying: "Plant this in a flowerpot,...
full_text:
Once upon a time, a lonely woman who longed for a little child sought counsel from a wise old woman. The old woman gave her a magic barleycorn, saying: "Plant this in a flowerpot, and watch what blossoms."

The woman planted the grain, and immediately a splendid red tulip shot up. Inside the closed petals sat a tiny, delicate maiden, no longer than a person's thumb. She was named Thumbelina. Her cradle was a polished walnut shell, her mattress was blue violet petals, and her counterpane was a fragrant rose leaf.

One night, an ugly, slimy toad hopped through a broken windowpane and carried off Thumbelina's walnut cradle to the marshy riverbank. "Croak, croak, brek-ek-kex!" rasped the old toad, planning to marry the tiny maiden to her clumsy son. They placed Thumbelina on a broad water-lily leaf in the middle of the stream so she could not escape. Thumbelina wept bitter tears of sorrow.

Hearing her cries, the little fish swimming beneath the water resolved that so sweet a child must never marry an ugly toad. They nibbled through the green stalk of the water-lily pad, and the leaf floated freely down the sparkling river, carrying Thumbelina away through sunshine and dancing butterflies.

Summer passed happily as Thumbelina lived in the great forest, drinking nectar from clover and sleeping under a broad burdock leaf. But when bitter winter arrived, the green leaves withered, snow fell in heavy flakes, and Thumbelina shivered in the freezing blast.

Numb with cold, she stumbled upon the underground burrow of an old field mouse. The kindly field mouse took pity on the shivering girl: "Come into my warm room, eat a grain of corn, and tell me stories through the long winter."

In the dark subterranean tunnels lived their neighbor, a wealthy mole dressed in black velvet who despised the sun and flowers. In the passage, Thumbelina discovered a swallow lying motionless, frozen by the sudden frost. The mole kicked the bird contemptuously, but Thumbelina's heart ached with tenderness. That night, she wove a blanket of soft hay, covered the cold swallow, and pressed her cheek against its chest. To her astonishment, she felt a faint, slow heartbeat! The swallow was not dead, only numbed by the bitter chill.

All winter, Thumbelina secretly tended the bird with warm water and soft moss. When spring's golden sun returned, the swallow revived, thanked his little savior with joyful chirps, and flew up into the open sky.

Soon, the field mouse announced that Thumbelina must marry the blind mole and live forever underground in the sunless earth. Thumbelina wept, begging to step into the daylight one last time to bid farewell to the radiant sun.

Suddenly, she heard a sweet twit-twit overhead. It was her beloved swallow! "The cruel winter is over," sang the bird. "Climb onto my back, dear Thumbelina, and let me carry you over mountain and sea to sunny southern lands!"

Thumbelina gladly mounted the swallow's feather back. They soared high above snow-capped peaks and azure oceans until they arrived in a paradise of blooming myrtle and marble palaces. The swallow placed Thumbelina upon a white blossom. In the center of the flower sat a tiny prince with a golden crown and translucent wings—the King of the Flower Spirits!

The prince fell instantly in love with Thumbelina's gentleness, placed his golden crown upon her head, and gave her a pair of delicate wings so she could fly from blossom to blossom in eternal sunshine and joy.
moral: Gentleness of heart and kindness to the helpless guide us through dark trials toward true belonging and light.

title: The Naughty Boy
summary: Once upon a time, an old poet sat by his cozy hearth on a stormy evening. Outside, rain beat furiously against the windowpanes, and the wind howled through the chimney like a wound...
full_text:
Once upon a time, an old poet sat by his cozy hearth on a stormy evening. Outside, rain beat furiously against the windowpanes, and the wind howled through the chimney like a wounded beast.

"How fortunate I am to sit here in the warm shelter of my study," said the old poet to himself, stirring the glowing embers.

Suddenly, a faint knock sounded at the door, accompanied by a child's plaintive cry: "Open the door, kind sir! I am shivering with cold, and the rain has soaked through all my clothes!"

The tender-hearted poet hastened to unbolt the door. There stood a little boy, completely naked, shivering from head to foot. Rain dripped from his golden curls, his lips were blue with frost, and behind his shoulders hung a pair of delicate, sodden wings. In his small hands, he held a tiny wooden bow and a quiver of painted arrows.

"Poor little creature!" said the poet with fatherly compassion. He carried the child to the fireside, warmed his freezing hands in his own, wrapped him in a warm dry woolen blanket, and fed him sweet wine and roasted apples.

The boy soon revived. The rosy color returned to his cheeks, his eyes sparkled with mischievous merriment, and he began to jump about the rug in high spirits.

"What is your name, my cheerful little guest?" asked the old poet with a warm smile.

"My name is Cupid!" laughed the boy. "Do you not know me? Look, here is my bow! Oh, but alas, the rain has surely ruined my bowstring!"

The boy took up his bow, examined the taut hemp, placed a sharp little arrow upon the notch, drew the string back to his ear, and aimed straight at the old poet's chest. Twang! The arrow pierced the poet right through the heart!

"Ha, ha, ha!" laughed the naughty boy, clapping his hands and dancing with glee. "My bowstring was not spoiled after all!" And with that, he spread his golden wings and flew straight out through the window into the stormy night.

The old poet lay clutching his wounded chest, for the arrow was tipped with love's burning fire. "Fie upon that treacherous boy!" he groaned. He warned all his young friends never to open their doors to the cunning little archer, but Cupid wanders the world in disguise to this very day, shooting his mischievous darts into unsuspecting hearts.
moral: Beware the unpredictable arrows of sudden infatuation, for passion often hides behind the guise of helplessness.

title: The Travelling Companion
summary: Poor Johannes was left entirely alone in the world when his beloved father died. He inherited only fifty silver coins, but he was good, pious, and resolved to walk through the wide...
full_text:
Poor Johannes was left entirely alone in the world when his beloved father died. He inherited only fifty silver coins, but he was good, pious, and resolved to walk through the wide world with an honest heart.

During his travels, Johannes entered a roadside church on a stormy evening. Inside, he found a dead man lying in an open coffin, while two angry ruffians prepared to toss the corpse into the muddy street. "He owed us fifty silver coins," they snarled, "and since he died without paying, his body shall rot in the ditch!"

Johannes could not bear to see a fellow Christian dishonored. He handed his entire inheritance—all fifty silver coins—to the creditors, leaving himself penniless, and saw the dead man buried with solemn dignity.

The next morning, as Johannes walked through the forest, a vigorous young stranger joined him on the road. "May I be your travelling companion?" asked the stranger. Johannes gladly accepted, and the two became sworn brothers. The mysterious companion possessed wonderful secrets: he healed a crippled girl with a magical ointment, collected three willow wands, and preserved the wings of a giant falcon.

They reached a splendid kingdom whose princess was renowned for breathtaking beauty, but possessed a cruel, bewitched heart. Any suitor who sought her hand was compelled to answer three riddles; failure meant beheading. Hundreds of bleached skulls already lined the palace palisade.

Johannes caught sight of the princess and loved her instantly. He stepped forward to accept the deadly trial. That night, the travelling companion strapped on the falcon's wings, flew silently after the princess as she flew to a secret cavern beneath a mountain, and observed her conferring with a wicked mountain sorcerer.

On the first morning, the princess asked: "What am I thinking of?" Johannes, instructed by his companion, replied: "Your silken glove!" On the second morning, he answered: "Your jeweled shoe!"

On the third night, the companion followed the princess into the mountain once more, slew the wicked sorcerer with his willow wands, and brought the severed head of the wizard in a silk scarf to Johannes. When the princess asked her final riddle: "What am I thinking of?", Johannes held up the sorcerer's head! The spell broke instantly; the princess's dark enchantment dissolved into tears of repentance and pure love.

The royal wedding was celebrated with great joy. At the feast, the companion turned to Johannes: "I was the dead man whose corpse you redeemed with your last fifty coins in the lonely church. I have repaid my debt of gratitude, and now I must return to my heavenly rest." With a radiant smile of peace, the companion vanished into thin air, leaving Johannes and his queen to rule in wisdom and righteousness.
moral: Kindness shown to the departed and the helpless returns in times of peril as an invincible guardian.

title: The Little Mermaid
summary: Far out at sea, where the water is as blue as cornflowers and as clear as crystal, lies the kingdom of the Sea King. His palace was built of coral with roof shingles made of pearl-...
full_text:
Far out at sea, where the water is as blue as cornflowers and as clear as crystal, lies the kingdom of the Sea King. His palace was built of coral with roof shingles made of pearl-bearing oyster shells. Here lived six lovely mermaid princesses, but the youngest was the fairest of all. Her skin was as delicate as a rose petal, her eyes as blue as the deep ocean, and her voice the sweetest music in the world.

When a mermaid reached her fifteenth year, she was permitted to rise to the surface to look upon the world of humans. When the little mermaid's turn came, she saw a magnificent three-masted ship where a handsome young prince celebrated his birthday under blazing fireworks. Suddenly, a ferocious tempest arose; lightning cleaved the dark sky, and monstrous waves broke the ship in two. The little mermaid saw the prince sink into the churning depths. Knowing mortals cannot live in the ocean, she dove fearlessly through floating beams and crushing breakers, lifted the unconscious prince above the water, and carried him gently to the sands of a peaceful shore near a white temple convent. A maiden came from the temple, and the prince opened his eyes, believing the stranger had saved him. The mermaid slipped sorrowfully back into the sea.

Yearning for the prince and longing for an immortal soul—which mortals possess but merfolk do not—the little mermaid visited the dreaded Sea Witch. The witch brewed a potent potion: "Drink this, and your fish's tail will divide into human legs. But every step you take will feel as if you are treading upon sharp knives, and your feet will bleed! In exchange for this potion, you must give me your voice—the sweetest voice on earth. I will cut out your tongue! And remember: if the prince marries another, you will never gain an immortal soul, but will dissolve on the following dawn into foam upon the waves!"

The little mermaid embraced the agonizing sacrifice for love. She drank the draught on the prince's palace shore, collapsing as a sharp blade seemed to cut through her body. The prince found the silent, beautiful maiden, clothed her in silk, and gave her a home in his palace. Though every step brought excruciating pain, she danced before him with airy grace that enchanted all who beheld her. The prince loved her as a dear sister, but his heart was pledged to the unknown temple maiden who had found him on the shore.

Soon, the prince's father arranged a marriage with the daughter of a neighboring king. When the bride arrived, the prince rejoiced, for she was the very maiden from the temple! The wedding took place aboard the royal ship amid music and golden banners. The little mermaid's heart broke, knowing that the rising sun would turn her into sea foam.

In the dead of night, her five mermaid sisters rose from the ocean waves. Their long golden hair had been shorn: "We have given our hair to the Sea Witch for this magical dagger! Drive it into the prince's heart before dawn, and his warm blood falling upon your feet will turn them back into a tail; you will live three hundred years as a mermaid!"

The little mermaid stood over the sleeping prince. She looked upon his peaceful face, murmured his name in silent devotion, kissed his brow, and cast the sharp knife far out into the waves. Then she cast herself into the sea.

As the dawn sun broke over the water, she did not dissolve into cold nothingness. She was lifted into the air by luminous beings of light—the Daughters of the Air. "Your selfless love and sacrifice have freed you," they sang. "By striving with your whole heart and enduring suffering without malice, you have won the path to an immortal soul!" And the little mermaid soared upward into the golden heavens, blessed with eternal life.
moral: True love does not seek to possess, but gives itself entirely, earning through sacrifice the light of an immortal soul.

title: The Emperor's New Clothes
summary: Many years ago, there lived an Emperor who cared so exceedingly for splendid new clothes that he spent all his revenues upon royal dress. He took no care of his soldiers, paid no h...
full_text:
Many years ago, there lived an Emperor who cared so exceedingly for splendid new clothes that he spent all his revenues upon royal dress. He took no care of his soldiers, paid no heed to the theater, and drove out into the park only to display his newest embroidered coats. He had a coat for every hour of the day; and just as people say of a king, "He is in his council chamber," so here they always said, "The Emperor is in his dressing room!"

One fine day, two cunning swindlers arrived in the capital. They announced that they were master weavers capable of producing the most extraordinary fabric imaginable: cloth of dazzling colors and intricate patterns that possessed the miraculous property of being completely invisible to anyone who was either hopelessly unfit for his post or unpardonably stupid!

"What capital clothes those would be!" thought the Emperor. "By wearing them, I could discover which men in my realm are unfit for their offices, and distinguish the wise from the foolish!" He paid the two impostors a vast sum of gold and provided heaps of fine silk and spun gold thread, which the rascals stuffed into their own knapsacks, setting up empty looms to work day and night at imaginary cloth.

Anxious to see how the fabric was progressing, the Emperor sent his honest old Prime Minister to inspect the work. The old minister peered at the empty frames: "Heaven preserve me!" he thought, rubbing his spectacles. "I cannot see a single thread!" But terrified of being branded stupid or incompetent, he nodded vigorously: "Oh, it is magnificent! Such exquisite patterns, such radiant colors! I shall report its perfection to His Majesty immediately."

Other court officials were dispatched, and each, trembling for his reputation, praised the non-existent fabric with extravagant eloquence.

At last, the Emperor came himself with his grand retinue. The swindlers raised their empty arms: "Look, Your Imperial Majesty! See the texture, feel the lightness; it is light as a spider's web!" The Emperor saw nothing, but thought in panic: "Can it be that I am a fool? Am I unfit to be Emperor? That would be the most dreadful thing on earth!" So he exclaimed: "Oh, it is beautiful! It has our highest imperial approval!"

The swindlers pretended to cut the cloth with huge scissors and sew it with needleless thread. On the morning of the grand imperial procession, they dressed the Emperor in his invisible robes.

The Emperor marched proudly under his royal canopy through the crowded streets. The courtiers carried the invisible train high in the air, and the populace shouted: "How incomparable are the Emperor's new clothes! How magnificent the train!" No one would confess he saw nothing, for that would prove him a fool or unfit for his office.

Suddenly, a little child in the crowd piped up with clear, innocent laughter:

"But he hasn't got anything on!"

"Listen to the voice of innocence!" gasped the child's father. A whisper ran like wildfire through the throng: "He has nothing on! A little child says he has nothing on!"

"He has nothing on!" roared the entire multitude at last.

The Emperor shivered, for he knew in his heart that they were right. But he thought: "The procession must go on!" So he held himself stiffer and prouder than ever, and his chamberlains walked on, carrying the train that wasn't there at all.
moral: Fear of looking foolish often leads crowds into absurd delusion; the honest voice of innocence dispels mass hypocrisy.

title: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
summary: There were once five-and-twenty tin soldiers, all brothers, for they were born of one old tin spoon. They held muskets at their shoulders, wore handsome red and blue uniforms, and...
full_text:
There were once five-and-twenty tin soldiers, all brothers, for they were born of one old tin spoon. They held muskets at their shoulders, wore handsome red and blue uniforms, and looked straight ahead with military discipline.

One soldier among them was slightly different from the rest: he had only a single leg, for he had been cast last and the melted tin had run short. Yet he stood as firmly and proudly on his one leg as his brothers did on two.

On the nursery table stood a charming paper castle with little windows through which mirrors looked like ponds surrounded by wax swans. In the open doorway stood a lovely little paper dancer. She stretched out her arms and lifted one leg so high in a graceful arabesque that the tin soldier could not see it, and thought she, too, possessed only a single leg! "What a splendid wife she would make for me!" sighed the steadfast tin soldier. He could not take his eyes from her.

When midnight struck, an ugly little black goblin popped out of a snuffbox. "Tin soldier," snarled the goblin, "keep your eyes to yourself!" But the soldier looked straight ahead and held his peace.

The next morning, the children placed the soldier on the window ledge. Whether by the wind or the goblin's malice, the window flew open, and down tumbled the soldier from the third floor, head first into the street, his bayonet lodging between the paving stones.

Two street urchins found him in the rain, folded a boat out of newspaper, and launched him down the swirling gutter. The paper boat spun dizzily into a dark sewer culvert where a giant water rat barked: "Show your passport!" But the soldier remained silent and steadfast, holding his musket firm.

The culvert emptied into a roaring canal; the fragile paper boat filled with water, dissolved, and the tin soldier sank into the depths. A giant fish swallowed him whole.

In the pitch-black belly of the fish, the steadfast soldier still lay upright with his musket across his chest. Later, the fish was caught, taken to market, and purchased by the very cook of the house where the soldier had lived! The cook cut the fish open with a carving knife, and cried: "Look! Here is the little tin soldier!"

He was placed back on the nursery table. There stood the castle, and there stood the exquisite paper dancer, still balancing on one leg. Their eyes met in silent, deep emotion.

Suddenly, a boy tossed the soldier into the blazing parlor stove without cause—surely prompted by the spiteful goblin. The soldier stood in the fierce glow, feeling an intense heat, though whether from the fire or from his burning love he could not tell. His bright uniform melted away, but he looked upon the dancer and remained steadfast. A sudden draft caught the little paper dancer; she fluttered like a sylph straight into the stove to his side, flashed into a bright spark, and was gone.

The next morning, when the maid raked out the ashes, she found the tin soldier melted into the shape of a little tin heart, and beside it lay the dancer's tinsel spangle, burned black as coal.
moral: Steadfast loyalty and unwavering dignity in the face of misfortune elevate the spirit above physical destruction.

title: The Wild Swans
summary: Far away in a kingdom where the sun warms the earth, lived a king who had eleven noble sons and one daughter named Elisa. The princes wore golden stars on their breasts and rode up...
full_text:
Far away in a kingdom where the sun warms the earth, lived a king who had eleven noble sons and one daughter named Elisa. The princes wore golden stars on their breasts and rode upon thoroughbred horses; Elisa read books illuminated with pictures of kings and fairies.

Their happiness ended when the king married a wicked queen who practiced sorcery. The stepmother hated the children: she sent Elisa to live with poor peasants in the forest, and cast an evil spell upon the eleven princes: "Fly away into the wilderness as wild birds without speech!" With a rushing sound, eleven splendid wild swans with golden crowns rose from the castle windows and vanished over the ocean.

When Elisa turned fifteen, she set out to find her lost brothers. Guided by an old woman who had seen eleven swans wearing golden crowns fly toward the seashore, Elisa reached the rocky coast. At sunset, eleven magnificent swans descended from the clouds; as the sun touched the horizon, their feathers fell away, and they stood before her as her beloved eleven brothers! They wept in joyous reunion, but the eldest warned: "By day we fly as wild swans across the sea; only by night do we regain our human form. Tomorrow we must fly across the vast ocean to a distant land, and we cannot leave you behind!"

The eleven brothers wove a sturdy net of willow bark and rushes. At dawn, Elisa lay in the net, and the swans lifted her into the clouds, flying all day with superhuman stamina above the waves until they reached a high mountain cavern.

In a dream, the fairy Morgana revealed the only way to break the curse: "Gather stinging nettles that grow in graveyards; crush them with your bare feet, spin the fibers into thread, and knit eleven long coats of mail. When you cast these over the swans, the spell will be broken! But remember: from the first knot to the last, you must maintain absolute silence. If a single word escapes your lips, it will pierce your brothers' hearts like a dagger!"

Elisa awoke and began the agonizing task immediately. The nettles blistered her delicate hands and feet, but she bore the burning pain with silent love.

A king hunting in the forest discovered the mute, beautiful maiden in the cave, fell in love with her grace, and brought her to his capital to be his queen. Elisa wept for joy, but continued her secret knitting every night. The king's suspicious archbishop whispered that she was a witch who consorted with ghouls in the cemetery. When Elisa ran out of nettles and crept to the churchyard at midnight to gather more, she was condemned to be burned at the stake.

Even in the execution cart, Elisa did not speak a word. Her hands worked with feverish speed, completing the eleventh coat of mail. As the pyre was about to be lit, eleven wild swans swooped down from the sky, encircling the cart. Elisa threw the eleven coats over the swans!

Instantly, eleven handsome princes stood in their place! Only the youngest had a swan's wing instead of his left arm, because Elisa had not finished the last sleeve.

"Now I may speak!" cried Elisa with tears of joy. "I am innocent!" The eldest prince stepped forward and revealed her heroic sacrifice to the king and the crowd. As the assembly bowed in reverence, the firewood burst into a garden of blooming red roses, and the king led his beloved queen into an era of everlasting peace.
moral: Pure, patient devotion and silent endurance possess the divine power to break the darkest enchantments.

title: The Garden of Paradise
summary: There was once a king's son who read vast libraries of books, but longed above all things to discover the Garden of Paradise, from which mankind had been expelled....
full_text:
There was once a king's son who read vast libraries of books, but longed above all things to discover the Garden of Paradise, from which mankind had been expelled.

One stormy evening, while wandering in a primeval forest, he sought shelter in the Cavern of the Winds. Here lived an ancient mother whose four sons were the North Wind, the South Wind, the East Wind, and the West Wind. When the gentle East Wind returned from his travels, he announced that he had just visited the Garden of Paradise, where the Phoenix nested and eternal spring reigned.

The young prince begged the East Wind to take him there. The East Wind agreed, lifted the prince onto his broad shoulders, and flew across sapphire seas and golden mountains until they landed upon the luminous island of Paradise.

The garden surpassed all human dreams. The air was scented with celestial blossoms, rivers flowed with crystal nectar, lions walked peacefully beside gazelles, and the Fairy of the Garden welcomed the prince with radiant grace.

"You may dwell here in joy," warned the Fairy Queen, "but beware the fatal temptation! When I sleep beneath the Tree of Knowledge, you must not approach, nor touch my lips. If you yield to curiosity and kiss me, Paradise will sink into the earth, and you will be cast out into sorrow and death."

The prince vowed absolute obedience: "I have the courage and willpower of a thousand men; I shall never falter!"

For several days, he lived in bliss. But on the hundredth evening, as music drifted through the golden groves, the prince walked near the Tree of Knowledge. He saw the Fairy sleeping in celestial beauty. Passion and pride flared in his chest: "I am strong! A single kiss can bring no harm!" He leaned over and kissed her lips.

A crack of thunder rent the sky like the doom of the world! Lightning tore the golden palace to dust, the garden vanished, and the prince awoke in the cold, howling rain of the earthly wilderness, weeping for the paradise he had lost through the lack of a single moment of self-restraint.
moral: Curiosity divorced from self-control loses the highest blessings; self-mastery is the gate to paradise.

title: The Flying Trunk
summary: There was once a wealthy merchant's son who squandered his vast inheritance on foolish pleasures: paper boats made of banknotes and games played with gold pieces. Soon he was reduc...
full_text:
There was once a wealthy merchant's son who squandered his vast inheritance on foolish pleasures: paper boats made of banknotes and games played with gold pieces. Soon he was reduced to living in an attic with only four copper coins and an old pair of slippers.

A faithful friend took pity on him and sent him an old wooden trunk with the advice: "Pack your goods and set out!" But having nothing to pack, the youth climbed inside the trunk himself.

The trunk was no ordinary box—it was enchanted! The moment one pressed the lock, it flew through the air! Whisk! Up through the chimney it soared, carrying the youth high above the clouds straight to the distant land of the Turks.

Landing in a royal garden, he learned that the Turkish king had locked his lovely daughter in a high copper tower because astrologers had foretold she would be unhappy with her suitor. The youth flew in his magic trunk right up to her balcony window!

The princess was enchanted by the mysterious visitor who arrived through the clouds. The youth boasted that he was the Turkish god of the air, and enchanted her with poetic fables of love and constellations. The princess agreed to marry him, and her parents, the Sultan and Sultana, declared they would give their royal consent if he told them a truly marvelous story on the eve of the wedding.

The clever youth returned to his trunk, bought fireworks and Roman candles, and that evening gave the city a dazzling aerial spectacle that lit up the heavens. Then he addressed the royal court, telling a witty, profound tale about the domestic conversations of kitchen matches, the iron pot, and the tea-urn. The Sultan wept with joy, and the Sultana embraced him: "You shall marry our daughter tomorrow!"

Filled with triumph, the merchant's son went into the woods to celebrate. But a stray spark from the fireworks had smoldered within the wood of the magical flying trunk; it had burst into flames and burned to white ashes!

He could no longer fly to the high tower. The princess waited at her balcony in tears, while the merchant's son was forced to wander the earth as a poor beggar, telling stories for crusts of bread, mourning the bride and fortune he had lost through heedless carelessness.
moral: Careless vanity and bragging squander precious gifts; words without wisdom leave one empty-handed.

title: The Storks
summary: On the thatched roof of a village farmhouse sat a stork's nest. Father Stork stood proudly on one leg upon the chimney ridge, keeping watch, while Mother Stork brooded over four li...
full_text:
On the thatched roof of a village farmhouse sat a stork's nest. Father Stork stood proudly on one leg upon the chimney ridge, keeping watch, while Mother Stork brooded over four little fledglings with black beaks and tender down.

In the street below, a crowd of mischievous schoolboys gathered. A naughty boy named Peter pointed up at the roof and sang a cruel mocking rhyme:
"Stork, stork, fly away,
Your nest will burn by light of day!
Your wife will be killed on the chimney pot,
And all your little ones boiled in the pot!"

The young storks were terrified, pulling in their heads and asking their mother: "Will they burn our nest? Will they boil us in a pot?"

"Pay no attention to them," consoled Mother Stork gently. "Practice your wings, learn to fly with your father across the green marshes, and when autumn comes, we shall fly south to the pyramids of Egypt, where melons grow by the Nile and warm sunshine shines all day long!"

One boy among the schoolboys, however, whose name was Little Peter, spoke up against the cruelty: "Shame on you! It is wicked to torment helpless birds that do no harm to anyone!"

Autumn arrived, and the young storks learned to fly with majestic wingbeats. Before departing for Egypt, the storks remembered the boys. "Shall we have our revenge?" asked the young storks.

"Justice shall be done," said Mother Stork. "In the deep forest lies a secret pond where sweet little human babies sleep among water lilies until the storks carry them to loving homes. To the good boy, Little Peter, who defended us, we shall bring a beautiful baby sister; and we shall name all of you Peter after him! But to the cruel boy who mocked us, we shall bring nothing but a dry twig to teach him that unkindness brings an empty heart."

And with triumphant cries, the storks circled the village in majesty and flew south toward the land of the sun.
moral: Cruelty to the innocent brings shame upon oneself, while kindness earns lasting blessings.

title: The Elf of the Rose
summary: In the center of a fragrant rose garden lived a tiny, exquisite elf. He was so delicate that no human eye could behold him; behind his shoulders grew two translucent wings, and his...
full_text:
In the center of a fragrant rose garden lived a tiny, exquisite elf. He was so delicate that no human eye could behold him; behind his shoulders grew two translucent wings, and his bed was the softest rose petal.

One evening, he lingered too long enjoying the perfume of the blossoms until night fell and the rose petals closed tight around him. Flying out, he rested inside a honeysuckle bower.

Beneath the bower sat two young lovers: a sweet maiden and an honorable youth, saying a sorrowful farewell, for the young man was departing on a long journey across the sea. The maiden gave him a fresh red rose, and they embraced with pure tears.

As the youth walked into the dark woods, the maiden's wicked brother ambushed him from the shadows. Driven by greedy lust for the family inheritance, the brother struck the noble youth dead with a dagger, severed his head, and buried the body beneath a linden tree.

The tiny rose elf witnessed the murder from the folds of the slain youth's rose. Filled with grief and horror, the elf flew to the maiden's bedchamber while she wept in restless sleep. Landing gently upon her ear, the elf breathed the truth into her dream: showing her the murder, the treacherous brother, and the secret grave under the linden tree.

The maiden awoke, ran into the forest at dawn, uncovered the tragic grave, kissed her beloved's cold brow, and took a fragrant sprig of flowering jasmine from the spot to plant in a porcelain urn in her room. She watered the jasmine with her tears day and night until the plant blossomed into extraordinary fragrance, drawing its life from her devoted grief. When she withered and died of a broken heart, the wicked brother seized the fragrant jasmine urn for himself.

The tiny rose elf flew to the queen of the bees. Swarms of bees flew into the brother's bedchamber and stung the murderer to death, avenging the innocent lovers through the righteous wrath of the gentle flowers.
moral: Hidden wickedness cannot remain buried forever; nature itself conspires to expose crime and honor love.

title: The Saucy Boy
summary: Once upon a time, an elderly poet lived peacefully in a thatched cottage at the edge of the woods. He had lived through many years, loved wisdom, and spent his quiet evenings writi...
full_text:
Once upon a time, an elderly poet lived peacefully in a thatched cottage at the edge of the woods. He had lived through many years, loved wisdom, and spent his quiet evenings writing songs of virtue and nature.

During a torrential autumn storm, as the wind rattled the shutters and rain fell in sheets, a child's tearful voice cried from the porch: "Let me in, kind grandfather! The cold wind will freeze me to death!"

The poet unlatched the heavy wooden bolt. There stood a charming little boy, golden-curled and rosy-cheeked, with wings like butterfly feathers shivering on his shoulders. He held a small polished bow made of ash-wood.

The kind old man brought the child inside, wrapped him in a warm wool cloak, and dried his wet curls before the blazing logs. "Here, child, drink this warm milk and eat this honey cake," said the poet warmly.

As soon as the boy grew warm, his eyes flashed with impudent mischief. "My bowstring was soaked in the rain," said the boy casually. "I must test whether it has lost its spring!"

Before the old man could raise a hand, the saucy boy fitted a sharp golden arrow to the bowstring, drew it to his ear, and shot the poet right through the center of his chest!

"Ha, ha, ha!" cried the saucy boy as he leaped onto the table, clapping his little hands. "My bow is as strong as ever!" And with a burst of mocking laughter, he spread his wings and flew up the chimney into the dark.

The arrow pierced the poet's chest with the sudden sweet and bitter agony of unexpected passion. The poet clutched his heart, groaning: "Oh, what a treacherous guest! That was Cupid, the boy who shoots without mercy!" The old poet warned every young person in the town never to shelter the saucy archer, for his arrows bring unrest and sleepless nights to the calmest minds.
moral: Do not be deceived by the charm of reckless desires; guard your heart with wisdom.

title: Ole Lukoie (The Sandman)
summary: In the whole wide world, no one knows so many enchanting stories as Ole Lukoie—the gentle Sandman of childhood!...
full_text:
In the whole wide world, no one knows so many enchanting stories as Ole Lukoie—the gentle Sandman of childhood!

When evening falls and children sit quietly at table, Ole Lukoie comes tiptoeing softly up the stairs in his stocking feet. He wears a silk coat that shimmers with ever-changing colors—green, red, and blue—and under each arm he carries an umbrella. One umbrella is painted with beautiful pictures, which he opens over good children so they dream delightful tales all night long; the other has no pictures at all, which he opens over naughty children so they sleep heavily and wake without a single dream.

On Monday, Ole Lukoie visited little Hjalmar. With a gentle squirt of sweet milk into the boy's eyes, he made his eyelids heavy, tucked him into bed, and tapped the furniture with his magic wand. Instantly, the potted flowers grew into giant trees that met above the bed, the picture on the wall opened into a living landscape, and Hjalmar sailed down a crystal river in a toy boat carved like a swan, accompanied by singing birds and dancing princesses!

On Tuesday, Ole Lukoie brought the letters in Hjalmar's copybook to life. The crooked letters leaned against each other in comical distress, and the Sandman taught them how to stand upright with military pride.

On Wednesday, the rain outside transformed into a silver sea, and Ole Lukoie took Hjalmar aboard a great flagship where swallows delivered letters from home.

Night after night through Sunday, Ole Lukoie showed Hjalmar the beauty of nature, the dignity of duty, and the peace of a gentle heart. On the final evening, Ole Lukoie showed Hjalmar his brother—the other Ole Lukoie, whom mortals call Death. "He is not terrible as people paint him," said the Sandman softly. "He rides on a magnificent black horse with a cloak of stars, and asks only: 'How are your marks in your schoolbook of life?' To those who have done good, he grants a ride to the golden palace of eternity."

And little Hjalmar closed his eyes in peaceful trust, knowing that goodness and love make life beautiful both in waking and in sleep.
moral: A peaceful conscience and kind deeds bring sweet dreams of wonder and eternal hope.

title: The Swineherd
summary: There was once a poor young prince who ruled a tiny kingdom; yet his realm was large enough to marry on, and marry he would!...
full_text:
There was once a poor young prince who ruled a tiny kingdom; yet his realm was large enough to marry on, and marry he would!

His father's grave held a rose tree that bloomed only once in five years; but when it bloomed, its single blossom breathed a perfume so sweet that whoever smelled it forgot all sorrows. The prince also possessed a nightingale that sang so exquisitely that all the melodies in the world seemed collected in its throat.

The prince sent the rose and the nightingale in silver caskets to the emperor's daughter, hoping to win her hand.

When the imperial princess opened the caskets, she clapped her hands: "Oh, papa! How charmingly they are made!" But when she smelled the rose, she pouted with disgust: "Fie, papa! It is not made of porcelain or silk; it is a natural rose!" And when the nightingale burst into heavenly song, the princess turned her back: "Pah! It is a real live bird! Let it fly away!"

The prince did not lose heart. He stained his face brown, dressed in rags, and went to the palace gates, begging for work. The emperor appointed him imperial swineherd.

In his dirty hut near the pigsties, the prince constructed a marvelous little cooking pot hung with brass bells. When the pot boiled, the bells chimed a sweet waltz, and whoever held his finger in the steam could smell what was cooking in every chimney in the town!

The princess heard the music and sent her lady-in-waiting to inquire about the price. "The swineherd demands ten kisses from the princess!" reported the maid. The vain princess hesitated, but her curiosity conquered her pride: her ladies held out their skirts to shield her, and she gave the dirty swineherd ten kisses.

Next, the swineherd fashioned a musical rattle that played all the dance tunes of the world. The price? "One hundred kisses from the princess!"

As the princess stood in the pigsty kissing the ragged swineherd for the toy, the emperor stepped out onto the balcony, rubbed his spectacles, and saw the disgraceful spectacle. "Be off with both of you!" roared the emperor, driving them both out of the empire with his slippers.

The princess wept by the roadside: "Alas, miserable wretch that I am! If only I had accepted the noble prince!"

The swineherd went behind a tree, washed the grime from his face, donned his royal garments, and stepped forward in magnificent majesty. The princess fell on her knees before him.

The prince looked upon her with scorn: "I have come to despise you! You would not accept an honest prince, nor care for a genuine rose or a living nightingale; but you were ready to kiss a dirty swineherd in the muck for a silly plaything! Now keep what you have chosen!" And he marched back to his own kingdom, shutting the palace gates against her forever.
moral: Flippant vanity that scorns true beauty for superficial novelties inevitably loses all honor.

title: The Buckwheat
summary: Often after a violent thunderstorm, when people walk past a field of buckwheat, they notice that the stalks are scorched black as coal, as though a fire had swept over them. The co...
full_text:
Often after a violent thunderstorm, when people walk past a field of buckwheat, they notice that the stalks are scorched black as coal, as though a fire had swept over them. The country folk say: "The lightning has struck it!" But how came it that the lightning struck the buckwheat?

Beside a green meadow stood a large field of golden corn, a field of oats, and a field of buckwheat. The buckwheat was extremely proud, swelling with vanity: "I am as rich as the corn, and far more beautiful! My blossom is as fair as the apple tree; has anyone ever seen anything more magnificent than me?"

An ancient, venerable willow tree stood at the corner of the field, watching the landscape with quiet wisdom.

Suddenly, a terrifying storm gathered on the horizon. The sky grew dark as pitch, and heavy black clouds rolled over the plain. As the first thunder cracked, the modest rye, the oats, and the corn bowed their heads in humble reverence before the majestic tempest.

"Bow your head as we do!" whispered the golden corn.
"I have no need to bow!" boasted the buckwheat proudly.

"Bow your head!" rustled the ancient willow tree. "The angel of storms comes flying upon wings of lightning! Bow your head, or he will strike you down before you can ask for mercy!"

"I will never bend!" cried the haughty buckwheat, stretching itself stiff and tall, staring straight into the blazing heart of the flash.

There came a blinding burst of white fire! The thunder shook the foundations of the earth, and the tempest passed. When the sun broke through the clouds, the corn and oats lifted their heads, refreshed by the rain; but the proud buckwheat lay scorched, shriveled, and blackened to ashes, destroyed forever by its own obstinate refusal to bow before the storm.

The old willow tree wept tears of sap over the charred field, reminding all who passed that humility preserves life, while stubborn pride invites destruction.
moral: Arrogance and obstinate pride in the face of life's great storms lead to sudden and irreversible ruin.

title: Holger Danske
summary: In the deep, subterranean vaults of Kronborg Castle at Elsinore, where the ocean breakers roar day and night against the granite battlements, sits Holger Danske—the ancient sleepin...
full_text:
In the deep, subterranean vaults of Kronborg Castle at Elsinore, where the ocean breakers roar day and night against the granite battlements, sits Holger Danske—the ancient sleeping hero of Denmark!

He is clad in heavy iron armor, resting his head upon his folded arms on a great stone table. His beard has grown so long that it has grown into the solid marble slab! He sleeps in deep, silent slumber, dreaming of everything that happens in the land above.

Old grandfather sat in his cozy chair carving a wooden figurehead for a ship, while his little grandson sat at his feet, listening with wide, shining eyes.

"Tell me of Holger Danske, grandfather!" asked the boy.

"He is no mere myth, my child," smiled the old grandfather, polishing the wood. "Holger Danske is the spirit of Danish courage, honesty, and brotherhood. He does not stir in times of peace, but rests and watches. Yet let real danger threaten our land—let an enemy come to crush our freedom—and the stone table will split in twain! Holger Danske will tear his beard from the marble, stand up in giant stature, draw his great broadsword, and his blows will thunder across the earth until the freedom of our people is secured!"

The little boy looked up at the stars through the window, feeling his chest swell with pride: "I, too, shall be brave and true, grandfather! I will study hard, love my country, and stand like Holger Danske whenever truth and justice are threatened."

And in the dark vaults beneath Kronborg, the ancient warrior smiled in his sleep, knowing that so long as children carry honor and courage in their hearts, the land is safe, and Holger Danske may sleep in peace.
moral: The soul of a people never dies; quiet strength and vigilance protect the homeland through all generations.

title: The Bell
summary: At sunset, when the red glow lingered in the evening clouds, a mysterious, solemn sound was often heard echoing through the narrow streets of the city. It sounded like the chime of...
full_text:
At sunset, when the red glow lingered in the evening clouds, a mysterious, solemn sound was often heard echoing through the narrow streets of the city. It sounded like the chime of a great church bell, sweet and profound; yet no bell hung in the city steeple that could produce so heavenly a music.

The people said: "It is the Bell in the great forest!"

Many set out into the wilderness to find it. Some turned back after a mile, distracted by tea-gardens and sweet-sellers; others mistook the hoot of an owl or the croak of a marsh frog for the sacred melody.

On the day of their confirmation, two youths set out from the cathedral, drawn by the celestial music. One was a king's son, dressed in fine velvet and boots of leather; the other was a poor widow's boy, clad in a worn homespun jacket and wooden clogs.

They walked together into the primeval forest. The sweet sound grew louder, vibrating through the fragrant moss and ancient pines. Soon the path divided: one track led through thorny thickets and rocky crags, while the other wound through shady groves where sweet berries grew.

The prince took the difficult, sunlit mountain ascent, determined to reach the summit; the poor boy took the humble lower path through the damp forest glade. Each pursued the divine music according to his nature, pure of heart and free of vanity.

The prince climbed the rugged cliff just as the sun was setting in majesty. Below him lay the ocean, blazing like molten gold, and above arched the infinite sapphire sky. And lo! Standing on the highest peak of the rocks, bathed in the same golden light, stood the poor widow's boy! They had arrived at the exact same moment from different paths.

The two youths ran to each other, clasped hands in silent reverence, and looked up into the vast cathedral of nature. The great bell was not made of brass or bronze; it was the grand organ of the universe itself—the harmony of sky, sea, and earth singing praises to the Eternal Creator.
moral: The highest truth is reached not by status or pride, but when humble faith and dedicated pursuit unite before the divine.

title: Grandmother
summary: Grandmother is very old; her face is lined with countless wrinkles, and her hair is white as fresh snow; but her eyes are bright, mild, and clear like two stars, looking upon you w...
full_text:
Grandmother is very old; her face is lined with countless wrinkles, and her hair is white as fresh snow; but her eyes are bright, mild, and clear like two stars, looking upon you with boundless tenderness.

She knows the sweetest, most marvelous stories. She wears a dress of heavy silk with wide flower patterns that rustles softly when she walks. When grandmother sits in her armchair, she takes out her large black leather hymn-book, with silver clasps. Between the yellowed pages lies a dry, pressed rose, flat and faded.

Whenever grandmother looks at that withered rose, a gentle, wistful smile touches her lips, and tears gather in her eyes. The children ask: "Why do you weep over a dry rose, grandmother?"

Then grandmother strokes their curls and speaks softly of long-ago days: of the spring morning when a handsome youth placed that fresh rose in her hair, of sweet vows whispered under the blooming linden trees, and of the years of joy and sorrow that followed. The youth has long since passed into eternity, and the rose has lost its color; but the love that gave it remains as fragrant and fresh in her soul as the first dawn of youth.

One day, grandmother sat motionless in her chair; her eyes were closed, and a serene, holy peace rested upon her pale brow. They said that grandmother had fallen asleep in death.

They placed her in a white coffin, and laid the old black hymn-book with the faded rose under her quiet hands. And on her face was a smile of triumphant joy, as if she had awakened to eternal spring, reunited with her beloved in the sunshine of everlasting life.
moral: The love and gentleness of grandparents leave an eternal blossom in the garden of human memory.

title: The Darning-Needle
summary: There was once a darning-needle who thought herself so fine and slender that she fancied she was an embroidery needle of the highest nobility!...
full_text:
There was once a darning-needle who thought herself so fine and slender that she fancied she was an embroidery needle of the highest nobility!

"Take care that you hold me properly!" she squeaked to the cook's fingers. "Do not let me drop, for if I fall to the floor, you will never find me, so fine and delicate am I!"

"That's my business," said the cook, and she threaded the darning-needle with coarse kitchen twine to mend a hole in an old leather slipper.

"What common work!" snorted the darning-needle. "I shall break! I am too aristocratic for this!" And snap! She broke in two right in the eye. "There now!" she said proudly. "I told you so; I am much too fine!"

The cook dropped a blob of black sealing-wax on the broken needle's head and stuck it into her neckerchief to use as a brooch. "Now I am a scarf-pin!" exclaimed the needle with boundless vanity. "I knew I would rise to high office; fine quality always wins in the end!"

While leaning forward, the cook dropped the needle into the gutter. Down it sank into the dark mud alongside broken eggshells and street refuse.

"Here I sit in deep retirement," declared the needle to a broken bottle-neck lying beside her. "I am so exceedingly fine that I enjoy quiet philosophical seclusion. Look at those ignorant eggshells; they crack under the slightest pressure, whereas I am made of pure steel!"

A street urchin playing in the gutter spotted the shining point, picked up the broken needle, and stuck it into an old eggshell to float down the swirling canal.

"Ah! Now I travel in my own private yacht!" cried the darning-needle in ecstasy. "How aristocratic! How splendid!" But a heavy cartwheel rolled through the puddle, crushing both eggshell and needle deep into the mire.

Even as she was squashed flat into the dirt, the darning-needle whispered proudly: "I am so fine, so delicate, that the entire world must roll over me!" And there she lies to this day, puffed up with vanity in the gutter.
moral: Absurd vanity that imagines itself superior even when discarded in the gutter is the pinnacle of folly.

title: The Little Match Girl
summary: It was bitterly, piercingly cold; snow was falling fast, and the darkness of New Year's Eve gathered over the frozen streets of the city....
full_text:
It was bitterly, piercingly cold; snow was falling fast, and the darkness of New Year's Eve gathered over the frozen streets of the city.

In this bitter chill, a poor little girl walked barefoot through the snow, shivering and hungry. When she had left home, she had worn an old pair of her mother's oversized slippers, but she had lost them while dodging two racing carriages. Her little bare feet were red and blue with the biting frost.

In an old torn apron, she carried a bundle of matches, and held a small packet in her trembling hand. All day long, no one had bought a single box from her; not a solitary soul had given her a copper coin.

Light streamed from every window, and the savory odor of roast goose drifted into the frozen street, for it was New Year's Eve. She sat down in a narrow corner between two brick houses, tucking her little feet beneath her ragged dress to keep warm. She dared not go home, for she had sold no matches, and her harsh father would surely beat her; besides, their garret under the roof was almost as cold as the street, with wind whistling through the straw-stuffed cracks.

Her little hands were almost paralyzed with cold. "Oh, if I could only strike a single match against the wall to warm my fingers!" she thought.

Scratch! She drew a match across the stone. What a wonderful flame flared up! It burned with a warm, bright glow like a tiny candle. The little girl held her hands over it. It seemed to her as though she were sitting before a magnificent iron stove with polished brass knobs; how deliciously the fire warmed her shivering limbs! She stretched out her feet to warm them too—and the flame went out! The stove vanished; she held only the charred remnant of the match in her hand.

She struck a second match. The light fell upon the brick wall, and it became transparent as gauze! She looked straight into a festive dining room where a white tablecloth was spread with fine porcelain, and a roasted goose stuffed with apples and dried plums hopped down from the dish with knife and fork in its breast, waddling across the floor toward the starving child! Then the match flickered out, leaving only the damp, cold brick wall.

She struck a third match. She sat beneath the most glorious Christmas tree, adorned with thousands of glowing tapers and colorful pictures. The little girl reached out her hands—and the match went out. The Christmas lights rose higher and higher into the sky, turning into radiant stars. One star fell, leaving a long trail of golden fire.

"Someone is dying," murmured the child softly, for her beloved grandmother, the only soul who had ever loved her, had said: "Whenever a star falls, a soul ascends to God."

She struck another match against the wall. In the radiant brightness stood her gentle grandmother, looking upon her with boundless love and peace.

"Grandmother!" cried the little girl, reaching out her arms. "Oh, take me with you! I know you will disappear when the match goes out, just like the warm stove, the delicious roast goose, and the splendid Christmas tree!"

Desperate to keep her grandmother with her, the child struck all the remaining matches in the packet at once! A blaze of light burst forth, brighter than the midday sun. Never had the grandmother appeared so tall, so radiant, so beautiful. She took the little girl in her arms, and both soared upward in light and joy, higher and higher, far above the earth, where there was neither cold, nor hunger, nor sorrow—for they were in the presence of God.

In the cold dawn of the New Year, the child lay frozen in the corner between the houses, rosy-cheeked and with a peaceful smile upon her lips, surrounded by burned matchsticks.

"She was trying to warm herself," said the passersby pityingly.

No one knew the heavenly glories she had beheld, nor in what radiant splendor she had entered with her grandmother into the joy of the New Year.
moral: Compassion for the suffering poor is a sacred duty; in divine grace, the destitute find eternal warmth and peace.

title: The Goloshes of Fortune
summary: In a grand house in Copenhagen, two fairies attended a lively evening party. One was the fairy of Fortune, and the other was Care's handmaiden. The fairy of Fortune brought a pair...
full_text:
In a grand house in Copenhagen, two fairies attended a lively evening party. One was the fairy of Fortune, and the other was Care's handmaiden. The fairy of Fortune brought a pair of magical goloshes (overshoes): "Whoever puts on these overshoes will instantly find his wish granted, transported to whatever place, station, or era he desires!"

Care's handmaiden smiled sadly: "He will find only misery, for mortals know not what they truly need."

The magical goloshes were left in the hallway. A young legal clerk, leaving the party in the rain, mistakenly put on the goloshes. Yearning for the romantic chivalry of the Middle Ages, he stepped out and wished: "Oh, if only I lived in the glorious age of King Hans!"

Presto! He plunged knee-deep into deep, foul medieval mud! The gas lamps disappeared; pitch darkness engulfed the unpaved streets; ruffians brandished crude halberds, and when he tried to speak, no one could understand his modern Danish. Terrified, he scrambled back to the present day, kicking off the dreadful shoes in horror.

Next, a night watchman found the goloshes. Gazing at the sparkling stars, he wished he were a lieutenant, only to find himself instantly burdened with mountain-high military debts and dueling quarrels! Then he wished he were soaring among the moonlit craters, and found himself freezing in airless void.

A romantic poet wore them, wishing to be a skylark; but as a bird, he was promptly snared in a net, caged, and pecked by jealous canaries.

Finally, a tired young student put them on. Exhausted by examination anxieties and worldly disappointments, he sighed: "Oh, how peaceful must be the dead who sleep beneath the turf!"

Instantly, his heart ceased to beat; he lay cold and still in a church coffin, mourned by his mother. But the fairies returned, pulled the fateful goloshes from the youth's feet, and his breath returned. He sat up, embraced the light of day with tears of gratitude, and resolved never again to curse the precious gift of living life.
moral: Unreflective wishes for different times or stations bring only sorrow; true peace lies in accepting one's own life.

title: The Daisy
summary: Out in the country, close by the roadside, stood a pleasant country house surrounded by a painted wooden fence. Just outside the fence, in the soft green ditch, grew a little modes...
full_text:
Out in the country, close by the roadside, stood a pleasant country house surrounded by a painted wooden fence. Just outside the fence, in the soft green ditch, grew a little modest daisy.

The sun shone upon the humble daisy with the same warm love that it bestowed upon the magnificent, proud peonies and roses inside the garden. The little daisy opened its small white petals like rays around a tiny yellow sun, and looked up into the vast blue sky with boundless gratitude. "I can see the sun, I can feel the warm breeze, and I can hear the lovely lark singing high above!" whispered the happy flower.

Inside the fenced garden, tall red tulips and pompous peonies puffed themselves out, looking down their noses at the wild weeds in the ditch. The little daisy did not envy them in the least; it rejoiced in its own quiet life.

Suddenly, a skylark flew down from the clouds, passed right over the grand tulips, and landed in the grass beside the daisy! The bird pecked gently at the daisy's petals with its beak and sang: "How sweet is the soft grass, and what a lovely little flower with a golden heart and silver dress!" The little daisy trembled with pure, innocent joy.

The next morning, two boys came into the ditch with a sharp knife. They dug up a square patch of turf to place in the bottom of a birdcage—and right in the center of the sod stood the little daisy.

In the cage hung the captive skylark, imprisoned behind iron bars. The poor bird beat its wings against the wires, singing a mournful lament for the lost blue sky, the open fields, and its freedom.

The boys forgot to give the captive bird a single drop of water. By midday, the blazing sun beat down upon the cage. The skylark gasped with parched throat, thrusting its beak into the damp grass turf where the daisy grew. The daisy could not speak, nor could it offer water, but it breathed out its sweetest fragrance to comfort the dying bird.

When evening fell, the poor lark bent its head toward the flower and breathed its last. The boys came in the morning, wept bitter tears over the dead bird, and buried the skylark in a handsome little grave lined with leaves. But the patch of turf with the faithful little daisy, they threw out into the dusty road where the wheels rolled over it. Yet the daisy had fulfilled its holy mission: offering its gentle heart in love and comfort to the very end.
moral: True sympathy shares the suffering of others; heedless cruelty to the helpless leaves a trail of sorrow.

title: The Brave Tin Soldier (The Steadfast Spirit)
summary: Cast from the residue of an ancient tin spoon, the little soldier was missing his left leg, yet he stood with unyielding military precision, eyes fixed forward upon duty and honor....
full_text:
Cast from the residue of an ancient tin spoon, the little soldier was missing his left leg, yet he stood with unyielding military precision, eyes fixed forward upon duty and honor.

In the playroom where he stood, his gaze was captivated by a delicate paper ballerina poised before a miniature palace. Her paper arms were spread in graceful welcome, and her slender leg was raised in an arabesque so high that the soldier believed she, too, possessed but a single limb. A silent communion of spirit bound them across the nursery floor.

Though thrown from the third-story window by a mischievous goblin, swept through churning gutter floods in a fragile newspaper boat, confronted by fierce sewer rats, and swallowed by a deep-sea cod, the steadfast soldier never wavered. He gripped his musket tight against his shoulder and kept his heart anchored in courage and devotion.

When Providence returned him to the very room of his beloved dancer, their eyes met across the polished wood, speaking of perils endured and faith preserved. Even when cast into the roaring hearth fire, where his bright uniform dissolved into molten metal, the soldier stood firm, gazing upon his love until a sudden gust of wind swept her paper form straight into the flames to his side.

When the ashes were cleared in the morning sun, they found his tin form melted into a pure, indestructible heart, holding within its center the tiny golden spangle of the ballerina—a symbol of steadfast love that fire itself could never consume.
moral: Steadfast fortitude of soul outlasts the fleeting trials of life and melts into eternal love.

title: Thumbelina (The Flight to the Sun)
summary: Born from the heart of a magical tulip, Thumbelina was no taller than a human thumb, sleeping in a polished walnut shell and rowing with white horsehairs upon a plate of clear wate...
keywords: the little tiny or thumbelina variant
full_text:
Born from the heart of a magical tulip, Thumbelina was no taller than a human thumb, sleeping in a polished walnut shell and rowing with white horsehairs upon a plate of clear water.

Her delicate beauty drew the unwanted designs of the marsh toad and the blind, subterranean mole who despised the warmth of the sun and the melody of birds. Yet through every captivity, Thumbelina's gentle heart remained pure and untainted by despair.

During the freezing depths of winter, while sheltering in the field mouse's underground burrow, Thumbelina found a dying swallow numbed by the frost in a dark tunnel. Defying the cold and the mole's mocking scorn, the tiny maiden wove blankets of dry grass, covered the bird's shivering body, and pressed her cheek against its feathered chest until the warmth of her compassion revived the fading heartbeat.

When the tyrannical mole prepared to drag her into eternal darkness beneath the earth, the grateful swallow returned from the open sky. Riding upon the bird's feathered back high above snow-clad peaks and shimmering azure seas, Thumbelina was carried into the golden lands of perpetual summer, where the King of the Flower Spirits crowned her his queen, giving her wings of light to dance among the blossoms forever.
moral: Compassion shown in the winter of adversity blossoms into wings of joy and liberation in the spring.
