title: The Ugly Duckling
summary: It was so glorious out in the country! The summer sun shone brightly on the golden wheat and green oats; storks walked on long red legs, chattering in Egyptian, while water-lilies...
full_text:
It was so glorious out in the country! The summer sun shone brightly on the golden wheat and green oats; storks walked on long red legs, chattering in Egyptian, while water-lilies floated on the quiet canals.

Under the broad leaves of a burdock plant, a mother duck sat upon her nest waiting for her eggs to hatch. Crack! Crack! One after another, the eggshells burst open, and tiny yellow ducklings poked out their heads, crying: "Cheep, cheep!"

Only one enormous egg remained unhatched. An old duck visited: "That is a turkey's egg! Leave it alone, you will never teach it to swim!" But the mother duck sat patiently until at last, the giant shell cracked. Out tumbled a large, awkward, grayish fledgling, looking clumsy and strange.

"What an ugly, overgrown creature!" cried the ducks in the yard. When they led the brood to the pond, the strange gray bird swam with effortless grace, using his legs better than any other. Yet in the poultry yard, the turkeys pecked him, the hens bit his neck, and the servant girl kicked him away with her shoe. Even his own brothers and sisters hissed: "If only the cat would catch you, you hideous fright!"

Heartbroken, the poor duckling flew over the hedge and fled into the wide moor where wild ducks lived. Through the bitter autumn, hunters' guns echoed through the reeds, dogs leaped through the water, and the terrified duckling hid in the rushes. He fled to a peasant's cottage where an arrogant cat and a haughty hen mocked him because he could neither purr nor lay eggs.

Winter arrived with piercing frost. The pond froze thicker and thicker; the duckling was forced to paddle with all his strength to keep a small breathing hole open in the ice, until at last he grew exhausted, froze fast in the ice, and lay stiff as stone. A farmer broke the ice with his wooden clog, carried him home, and revived him by the kitchen stove.

When spring returned, golden warmth filled the earth. The larks sang, and the apple trees blossomed. The duckling flapped his wings; they beat the air with tremendous power and lifted him high above the green meadows into a magnificent royal garden.

There, gliding upon the mirror surface of a clear lake, swam three dazzling, majestic white swans with curved necks and snow-white plumage.

"I will fly to these royal birds," thought the lonely duckling. "They will surely peck me to death because I am so ugly, but it is better to be killed by them than to be bitten by ducks, pecked by hens, and starved by winter!"

He flew down to the water and swam toward the magnificent swans with bowed head, whispering: "Kill me!"

He looked down into the clear crystal water. What did he see reflected in the mirror below?

He was no longer a clumsy, dark gray, hideous duckling! He was a swan—a glorious, graceful, radiant white swan!

The other swans swam around him, stroking his feathers with their beaks in joyous welcome. Little children ran into the garden, tossing bread and sweet cake into the water, shouting with clapping hands: "Look! There is a new swan! And he is the fairest and most magnificent of all!"

He rustled his feathers, lifted his slender neck toward the blue sky, and whispered from the depths of his overflowing heart: "I never dreamed of such happiness when I was the despised ugly duckling!"
moral: It does not matter having been born in a duck-yard, if only one has lain in a swan's egg; patience reveals true beauty.

title: The Fir Tree
summary: Out in the deep green forest grew a charming little fir tree. It occupied a delightful spot, where the sun warmed its branches, the breeze played through its needles, and many tall...
full_text:
Out in the deep green forest grew a charming little fir tree. It occupied a delightful spot, where the sun warmed its branches, the breeze played through its needles, and many taller pine and spruce companions grew around it.

Yet the little fir tree was thoroughly discontented. It thought of nothing but growing taller: "Oh, if only I were a tall, majestic tree like my elders! The birds would build nests in my boughs, and when the wind blew, I could nod with aristocratic grandeur!"

The sweet sunshine, the gentle breeze, and the merry country children who gathered wild strawberries around its trunk meant nothing to the impatient tree. "Grow! Grow! That is the only thing worth living for!" it sighed.

In autumn, woodcutters arrived and felled several of the tallest pines. The swallows and storks told the fir tree that the great trunks were made into masts for magnificent ships that sailed across stormy oceans. "Oh, how glorious to cross the blue seas!" yearned the fir tree.

When winter approached, young fir trees were cut down and carried away in carts. "Where are they going?" asked the fir tree.

"We know! We know!" chirped the sparrows through the windowpanes. "We have seen them in the grand houses of the city! They stand in the center of warm parlors, adorned with hundreds of glowing tapers, gilded apples, gingerbread, and thousands of toys!"

"Ah!" cried the fir tree, trembling with desire. "That is my destiny! That is the summit of glory!"

At Christmas, the woodman's axe bit deep into the fir tree's root. It fell with a heavy groan, feeling sharp pain as it was dragged away. In the city mansion, servants placed the tree in a wooden tub filled with sand. Golden nuts, silk ribbons, gingerbread figures, and a glittering gold star upon its highest branch completed its adornment.

When the candles were lit, the room blazed like fairy land! The children rushed into the room, danced around the tree in ecstasy, stripped it of its sweetmeats, and cheered as the old grandfather told the story of Klumpey-Dumpey. The fir tree stood in pride: "Tomorrow I shall be dressed in glory once more!"

The next morning, the footmen carried the fir tree not to the parlor, but up the dark stairs into the dusty garret, shoving it into a gloomy corner. The tree stood in darkness for months, forgotten.

The little mice visited, squeaking: "Tell us a story, old fir tree!" The tree told them of the forest sunshine, the fresh morning dew, and the glorious Christmas Eve. As he spoke, he realized for the first time how sweet and precious those forest days had been.

In spring, the servants dragged the dried, yellowed fir tree into the courtyard. The sun shone warm, the swallows sang, and children played upon the lawn. "Now life begins anew!" thought the tree, stretching its branches. But its boughs were brown and withered. A servant seized an axe, chopped the fir tree into pieces, and fed them into the brewing copper stove.

As the wood cracked in the flames, each pop sounded like a quiet sigh: "It is past! It is past! If only I had rejoiced while I had the time! Rejoice in your youth, rejoice in your fresh life while it is yours!" And the last spark flickered out into gray ashes.
moral: Live joyfully in the present moment; longing for future glory or mourning the past blinds us to life's present blessings.

title: The Snow Queen
summary: Long ago, an evil hobgoblin created a magic mirror that had the dreadful property of making everything beautiful and good appear shriveled and hideous, while whatever was vile and...
full_text:
Long ago, an evil hobgoblin created a magic mirror that had the dreadful property of making everything beautiful and good appear shriveled and hideous, while whatever was vile and wicked appeared magnified. When the demon's apprentices attempted to fly the mirror to heaven, it slipped from their grasp, smashed against the earth, and shattered into billions of microscopic glass splinters.

In a great city lived two poor children who loved each other like brother and sister: little Kai and little Gerda. Their parents lived in adjacent attics, and between their windows grew a box of sweet red roses.

One winter day, as snow swirled against the panes, Kai looked through the glass. A tiny splinter of the demon's mirror pierced his eye, and another penetrated his heart!

Instantly, his heart turned cold as a lump of ice. He kicked over the rose boxes, mocked his grandmother, and sneered at little Gerda. That afternoon, Kai tied his sled to the grand white sleigh of the Snow Queen—a majestic lady draped in glittering white fur. She kissed his forehead, numbing him to cold, and bore him away to her frozen palace at the North Pole, where he sat trying to assemble the word "Eternity" from sharp shards of ice.

Little Gerda wept bitter tears. When spring returned, she put on her new red shoes and set out alone into the wide world to find her lost Kai.

Gerda journeyed with barefoot devotion. She was sheltered by an old woman in a garden of perpetual summer, aided by a wise raven and a noble prince and princess, and captured by fierce mountain robbers in a pine forest. But the fierce little robber girl was touched by Gerda's gentle tears, released her, and gave her a swift Lapland reindeer to carry her to the frozen North.

Through bitter blizzards, the reindeer bore Gerda to the Finmark woman, who said: "I can give her no greater power than she already possesses! Her power lies in her pure, innocent child's heart; because love rules within her, man and beast must serve her."

Gerda arrived alone at the vast, desolate palace of the Snow Queen. Howling frost giants barred the way, but Gerda murmured the Lord's Prayer; her warm breath formed angel legions that drove back the icy monsters.

She burst into the empty throne room where Kai sat frozen, stiff, and blue. She threw her arms around his neck, weeping tears of burning love.

Gerda's warm tears fell upon Kai's chest; they penetrated straight into his frozen heart, melted the lump of ice, and dissolved the evil demon's splinter!

Kai looked upon Gerda, burst into sobs, and wept out the glass splinter from his eye! He recognized his beloved friend, crying: "Gerda! Dear little Gerda! Where have you been, and where have I been?"

The ice shards danced of their own accord and spelled out "Eternity." Hand in hand, the children walked back through the melting snows, through the green forests and singing birds, until they reached their own city. The church bells were ringing, the roses bloomed outside their attic window, and they sat down together—grown into youth, yet retaining the innocent, eternal hearts of children.
moral: The innocence and pure love of a devoted heart possess the power to melt the coldest ice of worldly cynicism.

title: The Elder-Tree Mother
summary: A little boy had caught a severe cold from getting his feet soaking wet while splashing in the city gutters. His mother tucked him into bed and brewed a steaming pot of elder-flowe...
full_text:
A little boy had caught a severe cold from getting his feet soaking wet while splashing in the city gutters. His mother tucked him into bed and brewed a steaming pot of elder-flower tea to drive away the fever.

An old grandfather who lived upstairs came into the room with a cheerful smile: "Now drink your tea, child, and I will tell you a story."

"Tell me about the Elder-Tree Mother!" begged the little boy.

As the boy sipped the fragrant tea, the lid of the teapot lifted. Out sprouted fresh green leaves and clusters of white elder-blossoms, spreading wider and wider until a majestic blooming elder tree filled the bedroom! In the branches sat a smiling, gentle old woman with wise, friendly eyes, wearing a moss-green robe adorned with white elder flowers.

"I am the Elder-Tree Mother," she smiled, "whom the country folk call the Dryad of Memory."

She lifted the boy into the fragrant branches, and together they flew back through time to witness the golden wedding of an old sailor and his devoted wife. They saw the couple when they were young lovers carving their initials into the bark of an elder tree; they saw the sailor sailing through tropical typhoons, preserved by his wife's prayers; they saw children born, loved, and grown to maturity; and they saw the elderly couple sitting hand in hand in the golden sunset, surrounded by grandchildren.

"Life is a marvelous fairy tale," whispered the Elder-Tree Mother softly, "written by the hand of love and memory."

The next morning, the boy awoke completely cured, his cheeks rosy and cool. On the table sat the empty porcelain teapot, and beside it lay a single fresh, white elder blossom, filling the quiet bedroom with the sweet fragrance of eternal remembrance.
moral: The sweetest poetry of life is woven from the simple, everyday memories shared across generations.

title: The Elfin Hill
summary: A commotion stirred through the enchanted forest! Several giant lizards scurried across the hollow oak roots, whispering that the Elfin Hill was to be raised on four glowing pillar...
full_text:
A commotion stirred through the enchanted forest! Several giant lizards scurried across the hollow oak roots, whispering that the Elfin Hill was to be raised on four glowing pillars that very night to host a grand banquet for royal guests from Norway.

The old Elfin King's house was swept with rush-brooms and polished until the mica stones sparkled like diamonds. The kitchen roasted fat earthworms, spiced frog-legs, and brewed sweet mushroom mead. The King of the Dovre Mountains in Norway had arrived with his two wild, boisterous sons to seek brides among the Elfin King's seven lovely daughters.

The old Norwegian Troll King sat on the seat of honor, telling grand sagas of roaring waterfalls, pine-clad fjords, and granite crags until his eyes sparkled. His two sons, however, were ill-mannered louts: they threw roasted beetles on the polished floor, put their muddy boots on the table, and fell asleep snoring.

The seven elfin maidens demonstrated their accomplishments: the first could turn mist into silver silk; the second could play the harp so sweetly that the trees wept sap; the third could brew magical potions; the fourth carried poetry in her fingers. But the Norwegian Troll King dismissed them all until he came to the youngest daughter.

She could tell enchanting tales of every stone, leaf, and mountain spring in the world.

"You shall be my queen!" roared the delighted old Norwegian Troll King, ignoring his lazy sons entirely. "You shall sit upon my throne of granite and tell me stories through the long winter nights!"

And as the cock crowed at dawn, the pillars sank back into the earth, the hill closed its grassy dome, and the boisterous sons hurried back to their snowy crags, while the wise maiden found an enduring kingdom in the northern mountains.
moral: Pretentious vanity and pompous matchmaking often reveal the shallow nature of worldly pride.

title: The Red Shoes
summary: There was once a pretty, delicate peasant girl named Karen who was so poor that she had to go barefoot in summer, and in winter wore heavy wooden clogs that made her ankles red and...
full_text:
There was once a pretty, delicate peasant girl named Karen who was so poor that she had to go barefoot in summer, and in winter wore heavy wooden clogs that made her ankles red and sore.

An old shoemaker's wife made Karen a pair of shoes from scraps of red cloth. They were clumsy, but Karen thought them the most wonderful things in the world.

When Karen's mother died, an elderly lady took pity on the child, took her into her home, and gave her clean clothes. Karen grew into lovely maidenhood, but vanity began to fester in her heart.

On the day of her confirmation in the great church, Karen deceived the half-blind old lady and bought a pair of dazzling red morocco leather dancing shoes meant for a countess. Throughout the solemn service, while the bishop placed his hands upon her head, Karen thought of nothing but her red shoes, admiring their glossy shine upon the flagstones.

When the old lady fell critically ill, Karen neglected her nursing duties to attend a grand midnight ball in town. The moment Karen stepped onto the ballroom floor, the red shoes took complete control of her feet!

They danced her out through the palace doors, down the marble steps, and into the dark streets. Karen tried to stop, but the shoes were glued to her feet; she tried to turn left, but the shoes danced right. Out into the dark forest they whirled her, through thorns and briars that tore her skin, past the executioner's hut where an angel with a flaming sword blocked her path: "Thou shalt dance in thy pride until thy skin shrivels to bone!"

Weeping in agony, Karen danced through day and night, through rain and snow, unable to rest or sleep. Driven to utter despair, she danced to the executioner's cottage and begged: "Chop off my feet with your axe, for I can endure this torment no longer!"

The executioner severed the shoes with his blade; and lo! The severed red shoes, with little feet inside, danced away into the forest depths and vanished.

The executioner carved her two wooden crutches, and Karen devoted the rest of her life to humble labor and heartfelt prayers in the village church. When her soul was purified of all vanity, an angel appeared in the nave, touched her with a green branch, and carried her forgiven spirit into the eternal mercy of heaven.
moral: Obsessive vanity leads the soul into uncontrollable torment; humble repentance alone restores peace.

title: The Shepherdess and the Chimney Sweep
summary: On a parlor table stood an antique carved cupboard of dark mahogany, covered with intricate carvings of roses and grinning satyrs. In the center was carved the figure of a goat-leg...
keywords: the shepherdess and the chimney sweep
full_text:
On a parlor table stood an antique carved cupboard of dark mahogany, covered with intricate carvings of roses and grinning satyrs. In the center was carved the figure of a goat-legged general, whom the parlor toys called "General-Head-Sergeant-Goat-Legged-Chieftain-Corporal."

On the tabletop beside the mirror stood two lovely porcelain figurines: a delicate little shepherdess wearing a golden bodice and holding a shepherd's crook, and a handsome little chimney sweep with his ladder, as black as soot, but crafted from the finest porcelain. They were betrothed to each other, for they were both fragile and loved each other tenderly.

Trouble arose when an old nodding Chinese mandarin of porcelain, who claimed to be the shepherdess's grandfather, nodded his consent to the goat-legged general: "She shall marry the wooden general and live inside the dark mahogany cabinet!"

The little shepherdess wept porcelain tears: "I will not marry him! Come, dear chimney sweep, let us flee into the wide world!"

The brave chimney sweep guided her to the fireplace. Together they climbed up through the soot-black chimney, crawling past the iron flue-pipe until they reached the chimney top under the open night sky!

Above them arched the infinite heavens, filled with millions of sparkling stars, and below lay the rooftops of the sleeping city. The little shepherdess looked down upon the dizzying vastness and burst into sobs: "The world is too great! I cannot bear it! Take me back to the little table by the mirror, or my heart will break!"

The faithful sweep, loving her more than his own desire for freedom, gently guided her back down the dark chimney.

When they emerged onto the parlor table, they found the old Chinese mandarin lying in three broken pieces on the floor—he had fallen off the edge while pursuing them! The family glued the mandarin's neck with brass wire, but his head could no longer nod.

When the goat-legged general demanded his bride, the old mandarin could only sit stiff and silent. So the delicate porcelain shepherdess and her brave chimney sweep remained peacefully united on the table, loving each other until they were broken to dust.
moral: True devotion dares to face the vast unknown, yet cherishes the quiet home where love is nurtured.

title: The Top and the Ball
summary: A wooden spinning top and a leather ball lay side by side in a toy drawer. The top, painted in gay stripes of red and gold, proposed marriage to the ball: "Since we reside in the s...
full_text:
A wooden spinning top and a leather ball lay side by side in a toy drawer. The top, painted in gay stripes of red and gold, proposed marriage to the ball: "Since we reside in the same box, why should we not become sweethearts?"

The ball, stuffed with fine cork and encased in morocco leather, tossed her head with disdain: "Do you imagine that I would condescend to marry a wooden top? My father was a Spanish morocco slipper, and I have a cork inside me! Besides, I am virtually engaged to a young swallow who visits my window every morning!"

"You may brag as you please," thought the top, "but I can dance upon one foot and spin until I hum like an organ!"

The next day, a boy took the ball into the garden and struck it with a racket. The ball leaped high into the azure air, looking like a bird soaring toward the sun. On the fourth strike, the ball soared over the roof and disappeared into the clouds.

Years passed. The top was turned on a lathe and painted with real gold leaf, so that he became a golden aristocrat. As he spun merrily, he leaped into a dustbin.

There, in the filthy muck beside an old cabbage stalk, lay a sodden, swollen, unrecognizable object.

"Who are you?" asked the golden top.

"I am a lady of high birth," croaked the soggy object. "I was made of genuine morocco leather and stuffed with cork, courted by swallows! But for five years, I have lain rotting in the roof gutter until the rain washed me down here."

The top recognized his former love, but turned away his golden face in silence. The housemaid arrived, emptied the dustbin into the ashes, and threw the rotten ball into the furnace. And the top spun on, remembering that pride goes before a fall.
moral: Haughty disdain toward honest devotion often ends in the garbage heap of forgotten vanity.

title: Holger the Dane (Guardian of the Realm)
summary: Beneath the granite dungeons of Kronborg Castle, surrounded by the ceaseless thunder of the Sound, sleeps Holger the Dane. His iron armor has turned green with age, and his snowy b...
full_text:
Beneath the granite dungeons of Kronborg Castle, surrounded by the ceaseless thunder of the Sound, sleeps Holger the Dane. His iron armor has turned green with age, and his snowy beard has grown straight through the solid marble table upon which he rests his weary brow.

Above his vaulted tomb, Danish fishermen cast their nets, merchant ships unfurl their canvas, and children play along the battlements under the blue Scandinavian skies.

"Does he ever wake, grandfather?" asked the young apprentice carver.

"Only when Denmark faces mortal extremity," replied the old artisan, carving the mast-head of an oak ship. "Holger is no phantom of blood and slaughter; he is the spirit of Danish honor, quiet industry, and unyielding fortitude. When tyrants threaten our shores, the marble table will split asunder, and Holger will rise to stand like an iron fortress before our hearths."

And the boy felt in his own chest the beating heart of his ancestors, knowing that so long as truth, labor, and courage flourish among the living, Holger's broadsword shall never fail.
moral: True strength sleeps in times of peace, but awakens with invincible power when justice is attacked.

title: The Little Mermaid (The Soul of the Sea)
summary: In the sapphire depths of the ocean abyss, where coral branches bloom and pearls carpet the seafloor, the youngest daughter of the Sea King yearned for the higher world of humans a...
full_text:
In the sapphire depths of the ocean abyss, where coral branches bloom and pearls carpet the seafloor, the youngest daughter of the Sea King yearned for the higher world of humans and the eternal soul that outlives the ocean tide.

She gave up her melodious voice, endured the agony of walking upon razor-sharp blades, and watched in silent silence as the prince she had rescued from shipwreck wedded another. Yet when her sorrowing mermaid sisters brought the enchanted dagger of the Sea Witch, commanding her to slay the prince to reclaim her ocean life, the little mermaid refused to let hatred or self-preservation stain her love.

She kissed the sleeping prince's brow, hurled the murderous blade into the foaming breakers, and leaped into the deep.

Instead of dissolving into cold sea foam, her selfless sacrifice lifted her into the radiant company of the Daughters of the Air. Through three centuries of silent deeds of mercy and comfort to crying children, she was granted the eternal path to the Kingdom of Heaven—proving that love which gives all without demand receives everlasting life.
moral: Love that surrenders all possessiveness transcends mortal limits to achieve immortal glory.

title: The Nightingale
summary: In China, you must know, the Emperor is a Chinese, and all the people he has about him are Chinese. His porcelain palace was the most splendid in the world, surrounded by a garden...
full_text:
In China, you must know, the Emperor is a Chinese, and all the people he has about him are Chinese. His porcelain palace was the most splendid in the world, surrounded by a garden filled with golden bells that chimed when the wind blew.

Beyond the garden stretched a great primeval forest reaching down to the blue ocean. In these green trees lived a little nightingale that sang so gloriously that even the poor fisherman, burdened with heavy nets, stopped to listen, saying: "How heavenly that sounds!"

Travelers from all lands wrote books praising the porcelain palace, but all concluded: "The nightingale is the greatest wonder of them all!"

The Emperor read this in a book and commanded his court: "Bring this nightingale to court tonight, or the entire council shall be trampled upon their stomachs!" The frightened courtiers hurried into the forest. A little kitchen maid guided them to where the modest, gray-brown bird sat singing in the branches.

When brought to the imperial court, the nightingale sang with such heavenly sweetness that tears streamed down the Emperor's cheeks. The Emperor offered his golden slipper to wear around the bird's neck, but the nightingale smiled: "I have seen tears in the Emperor's eyes; that is the greatest treasure in the world."

The bird was given a golden cage and allowed to fly out twice a day, tied by silk threads to twelve footmen.

One day, a package arrived from the Emperor of Japan containing an artificial nightingale made of solid gold and diamonds. When wound up with a key, it sang a mechanical waltz and wagged its silver tail. The court was ecstatic: "It is far superior! It never tires, and its songs can be predicted beforehand!" The real nightingale quietly flew out the open window back to his green woods.

Years passed. One evening, as the mechanical bird was singing, something went "Whir-r-r!" inside; a spring snapped, and the music stopped forever.

Five years later, the Emperor lay critically ill. He lay pale and cold in his imperial bed, while courtiers whispered that he was dead. Upon his chest sat Death, wearing the imperial crown and holding the golden saber. Terrifying phantoms of his past deeds peered from behind the heavy velvet curtains: "Do you remember this? Do you remember that?"

"Music! Imperial court music!" groaned the Emperor. "Beat the drums that I may not hear these voices!" But the mechanical bird sat silent on its golden perch.

Suddenly, through the open window, floated a strain of celestial song! It was the little living nightingale, who had heard of his sovereign's distress and flew from the forest to bring comfort.

He sang of the quiet churchyard where white roses grow, where the elder tree smells sweet, and fresh grass is watered by tears. As he sang, Death felt a longing for his quiet garden, relinquished the crown and saber, and drifted out into the cold mist like a shadow.

Color returned to the Emperor's cheeks. "Heavenly bird!" wept the Emperor. "I drove you from my realm, yet you have sung Death away from my bed! How can I ever repay you?"

"You have repaid me already," sang the nightingale softly. "You gave me your tears when first I sang to you; I can never forget that. Sleep now and grow strong. I will visit your window at twilight to sing of those who suffer, of the fisherman and the plowman, and the truth hidden from kings. Only promise me one thing: let no one know you have a little bird who tells you everything."

The next morning, the attendants came in to look upon their dead sovereign—and the Emperor stood tall, smiling in royal vigor: "Good morning!"
moral: Mechanical artifice can mimic form, but only the authentic, living voice of the soul can conquer Death.

title: The Angel
summary: Whenever a good child dies, an angel of God comes down from heaven, gathers the sleeping child into his arms, spreads his great white wings, and flies gently over all the places th...
full_text:
Whenever a good child dies, an angel of God comes down from heaven, gathers the sleeping child into his arms, spreads his great white wings, and flies gently over all the places the child loved on earth.

Before soaring to the celestial gates, the angel gathers a large handful of wild flowers to plant in heaven, where they will bloom more radiantly than on earth.

As they flew over green fields and gardens, the angel gathered red roses, blue violets, and white lilies. But flying over a dark, narrow alleyway in the crowded city, the angel descended toward a heap of broken pottery and street refuse in the gutter.

There, lying among the broken shards, lay a dry, withered field marigold that had fallen from a cracked flowerpot.

"Why do you gather that poor, broken flower?" asked the child.

The angel smiled with heavenly tenderness: "In a dark cellar in this narrow lane lived a poor, crippled boy. From his childhood, he lay confined to his bed; on the finest summer days, the sunbeams touched the cellar floor for half an hour, and he would hold his pale hands in the light, saying: 'Today I have been out!'

One spring morning, a neighbor's boy brought him this wild field marigold with its roots intact. The crippled boy planted it in an old cracked earthen pot, watered it with loving care, and watched every leaf unfold. It was his garden, his companion, his little treasure on earth. He smiled at its yellow blossom and smelled its fragrance until the day God called his soul home.

When the boy died, the people cleared the cellar and threw the poor withered marigold into the gutter. But that humble flower brought more pure joy to a suffering soul than the rarest rose in an emperor's palace!"

"How do you know this so well, dear angel?" asked the child with wonder.

The angel looked upon the child with boundless love: "I know it, because I was myself that little crippled boy who lay in the dark cellar, and this was my beloved flower!"

And the angel kissed the child, and they soared together into the golden light of heaven, where the withered marigold bloomed forever in the garden of eternal peace.
moral: The humblest flower cherished in sorrow shines brightest in the garden of heaven.

title: The Sweethearts (Top and Ball)
summary: The brightly painted spinning top offered his faithful heart to the elegant morocco leather ball, only to be mocked and rejected with haughty pride. The ball claimed royal descent...
full_text:
In the corner of a sunny nursery, an array of toys lay resting inside an open cedar play-chest. Among them was a handsome wooden spinning top, turned from smooth beechwood and painted in brilliant rings of vermilion, emerald, and gold. Beside him in the chest lay a delicate ball made of fine morocco leather, stitched with silver thread and as bouncy as a feather on the wind. The spinning top gazed upon her round perfection with deep affection and said politely: "Dear lady, since we live together in the very same box and share the play of the children, shall we not be sweethearts and plight our troth?"

The leather ball bounced slightly upon the velvet lining and tilted her nose in haughty scorn. "Sweethearts, indeed!" she scoffed. "You forget yourself, little beechwood peg! Do you not know that my grandfather was a pair of genuine Spanish leather slippers belonging to a court countess, and that my inner core is made of pure cork from the forests of Portugal? Besides, I am virtually betrothed to a high-soaring swallow who visits my windowsill every dawn; whenever I bounce into the garden air, he looks down and sings of our upcoming wedding!" The top bowed his painted head in quiet sadness, yet his faithful heart continued to cherish her, spinning with sorrowful devotion whenever the boy whipped his cord.

Years rolled past, and the children grew into men. One sunny afternoon, the boy struck the leather ball with a tennis racket. She soared into the clouds, higher and higher, until she vanished over the copper rooftops and was never seen again. The wooden top, however, was retrieved by the master of the house, covered in pure gold leaf, and placed upon an ebony stand in the parlor as an antique treasure. Many seasons later, while the maid was clearing old rubbish from the rain-gutter, the top slipped down into the dustbin. There, wedged between a cabbage stalk and an old shoe, lay a blackened, soggy, misshapen lump of rotted cork. "Alas," sighed the decayed ball, not recognizing the golden top, "in my youth I was courted by kings, but here I rot in the mud!" The golden top recognized his former love, spun silently away with gentle sorrow, and thought how tragic is the fate of empty vanity that spurns sincere love only to end in the dustbin of regret.
moral: Spurning sincere affection out of pretentious vanity leads to the rubbish bin of regret.

full_text:
For many decades, an old street lamp had faithfully stood on the corner of a quiet street, illuminating travelers through rain, snow, and dense fog. Now the evening arrived when the city council was to decide its fate: whether it should be melted down into copper coinage or allowed an honorable retirement.

The old lamp was filled with anxiety: "I have known so many people; I lit the student on his way to fame, guided the physician to the sick, and protected the poor watchman!"

An old retired watchman and his gentle wife, who lived in a clean, modest cottage, remembered the faithful lamp. They petitioned the council, brought the old street lamp home, and placed it upon a polished wooden table by their fireside.

The lamp was polished until it shone like gold. Every evening, the old watchman trimmed its wick, and the old lamp shone with warm, clear light upon their cozy parlor, casting gentle rays upon their books and blooming geraniums, grateful that a life of honest public service had found a peaceful harbor of love.
moral: A lifetime of humble, faithful duty is rewarded with quiet retirement and warm friendship.

title: The Little Match Girl (The Vision of Peace)
summary: Barefoot in the New Year's Eve snowfall, the little match seller crouched between cold brick walls, her trembling fingers numbed by the bitter Scandinavian frost....
full_text:
It was bitterly cold; the snow fell thick and white over the cobbled alleys of Copenhagen, and the twilight of New Year’s Eve was gathering into the icy night. Through the frost and darkness walked a poor little girl, bareheaded and barefooted. She had possessed a pair of her mother's oversized slippers when she left home in the morning, but they were so large that she lost them while scrambling across the snowy street to escape two reckless carriages. In her tattered old apron she carried a bundle of matches, and she held a single packet tightly in her numb, blue fingers. All day long she had wandered through the streets, yet not a single passerby had purchased a match, nor dropped a copper into her trembling palm.

Shivering with cold and gnawing hunger, she crept into a narrow recess between two tall brick houses and curled her tiny legs beneath her thin skirt. Lights sparkled warmly through the frosted parlor windows, and the delicious scent of roasted goose drifted into the alley, for it was New Year’s Eve. Her little hands were almost dead with frost. 'If only I dared pull just one match from the bundle,' she whispered to herself, 'and strike it against the rough brick wall to warm my fingers!' She drew out a match—SCRITCH! How it flared and sputtered with golden fire! She cupped her hands around the warm flame. Suddenly, it seemed as though she sat before a splendid polished iron stove with polished brass knobs; the fire burned with wonderful warmth, and the child stretched out her cold feet to toast them. But pop! The flame vanished, the stove dissolved, and she sat with the charred match-end in her hand.

She struck a second match against the wall. The brickwork became transparent like a curtain of fine gauze, and she could see into the dining room where a white linen cloth was spread with porcelain dishes and a roasted goose stuffed with apples and dried plums. Miraculously, the goose hopped down from the platter, waddled across the floor with the carving knife in its back, and came right up to the starving child! Then the match went out, leaving only the damp, freezing wall. She struck a third match, and instantly sat beneath the most magnificent Christmas tree, adorned with thousands of glowing tapers and colorful pictures that smiled down upon her. As the child reached out her arms, the lights rose higher and higher into the sky, transforming into bright stars. One fell, trailing a golden tail across the black heavens. 'Someone is dying,' whispered the little girl, remembering her gentle grandmother, the only soul who had ever truly loved her, who used to say that a shooting star marks a human soul ascending to God.

She struck another match against the brick, and in the radiant glow stood her grandmother, looking so gentle, loving, and bright. 'Grandmother!' cried the child. 'Oh, take me with you! I know you will vanish when the match goes out, just like the warm stove, the delicious roast goose, and the Christmas tree!' Desperately, she struck the entire remainder of the packet against the brick, wanting to keep her grandmother near. The matches blazed with a light brighter than midday, and the grandmother had never appeared so grand or so beautiful. She took the little girl in her arms, and together they soared in brightness and joy, higher and higher, far above the cold, the hunger, and the cruelty of the world, into the presence of eternal peace. In the golden dawn of New Year’s morning, the townsfolk found the child leaning against the wall, with rosy cheeks and a serene smile upon her lips, holding the burned matchsticks. 'She was trying to warm herself,' whispered the people. But no one knew what glorious visions she had seen, or in what radiant joy she had entered the new year with her grandmother.

title: The Shadow
summary: In the hot southern lands, a learned scholar sat upon his balcony on a warm evening. Opposite his lodging stood a mysterious house where radiant flowers bloomed and enchanting musi...
full_text:
In the hot southern lands, a learned scholar sat upon his balcony on a warm evening. Opposite his lodging stood a mysterious house where radiant flowers bloomed and enchanting music echoed through the night. The scholar humorously told his shadow: "Go across the street and see what is inside!"

The shadow obeyed: it detached itself from the scholar's feet, crossed the street, and disappeared through the opposite doorway!

Years passed. The scholar returned to his northern homeland, writing noble books on truth, beauty, and virtue; but people cared little for his deep philosophy.

One evening, a wealthy, haughty gentleman knocked at his study door. It was his former shadow! Dressed in fine clothes, adorned with diamonds and gold chains, the shadow had learned all the shameful secrets and private vices of humanity, becoming immensely wealthy through blackmail and flattery.

"I have become a master of the world," boasted the shadow. "You, my dear scholar, are poor and neglected. Travel with me as my companion; you shall have fine food, but you must pretend that you are my shadow!"

The noble scholar refused to live a lie. But the shadow had won the favor of a foreign princess who suffered from the disease of seeing too clearly. The cunning shadow persuaded the princess to marry him, and denounced the honest scholar as a madman who claimed to be his master!

On the night of the royal wedding, while bells rang and wine flowed in the palace, the honest scholar was quietly executed in the prison dungeon. And the triumphant shadow reigned over the empire—a chilling warning of what happens when superficial illusion conquers substance and truth.
moral: When superficial appearances and cynical cunning usurp the place of truth and intellect, humanity falls into servitude.

title: The Old House

full_text:
On a modern street of tall, new brick buildings stood a venerable old house built three hundred years earlier. Its gables were carved with grinning knights and climbing vines, its leaded windows were narrow, and brass gutters sprouted water-dragons.

Across the street lived a cheerful little boy who loved looking at the picturesque antique building. In the bay window sat an old man with silver hair and knee-breeches, living in solitary retirement.

Feeling that the old gentleman must be lonely, the little boy wrapped one of his precious tin soldiers in paper and sent it across the street with the maid as a present.

The old man was overjoyed by the child's tender thought. He invited the boy to visit the antique home, where gilded leather tapestries whispered stories from the walls, family portraits smiled, and an ancient piano chimed sweet melodies of long-ago days.

The tin soldier lived in the old house, keeping the lonely elder company until the old man passed peacefully away. Years later, when the old house was demolished and a new garden planted, the boy—now a grown man with a loving family—found the rusted tin soldier buried in the earth, and felt his heart fill with gratitude for the timeless lessons of friendship across generations.
moral: Honoring the elderly with youthful kindness brings warmth to lonely years and seeds memories for the future.

title: The Drop of Water

full_text:
Old Krible-Krable was an eccentric philosopher who spent his life peering through powerful magnifying lenses at the microscopic world.

One afternoon, he dipped a glass slide into a murky ditch-puddle, placed it under his great microscope, and invited his friend to look.

Thousands of tiny, fierce creatures swam and wrestled within the single drop of water! They bit off each other's limbs, swallowed one another whole, and fought furiously over every microscopic speck of weed.

"What a monstrous, bloodthirsty city this must be!" gasped the visitor. "Look at those generals conquering their neighbors, and those mobs tearing down their fellows!"

"It is no great city of men," laughed old Krible-Krable with a wry smile. "It is merely a single drop of ditch-water! Yet how like the great capitals of human pride it appears, where mortals fight and rage over fleeting trifles, blind to the vast universe that arches above them!"
moral: Looking upon human strife through the lens of wisdom reveals the pettiness of selfish conflict.

full_text:
Under the broad, leafy forest of burdock plants in an abandoned manor garden lived the last two venerable white snails. They were the aristocracy of their kind, possessing hard, smooth, ribbed shells, and their ancestors had once been served on silver platters in the grand castle.

The old snail couple had adopted a little orphan snail, whom they raised with tender pride. "Our burdock forest was planted solely for us," declared Father Snail. "And when our son is grown, he shall marry a fine snail maiden and inherit the burdock kingdom!"

They arranged a betrothal with an industrious young maiden snail from a neighboring gooseberry bush. The wedding was celebrated with great joy: the glowworms lit the burdock leaves, the black beetles drummed upon dry twigs, and the happy couple crawled side by side across the moist loam.

When Father and Mother Snail retired peacefully into their shells for their long sleep, the young snails lived in joyful harmony, declaring that their leafy canopy was the finest castle in the world.
moral: True contentment lies in rejoicing in one's own home and family without craving artificial grandeur.

title: The Story of a Mother
summary: A mother sat watching by the cradle of her sick child, her heart heavy with dread. A faint knock sounded at the door, and an old man wrapped in a black horse-cloth entered, shiveri...
full_text:
A mother sat watching by the cradle of her sick child, her heart heavy with dread. A faint knock sounded at the door, and an old man wrapped in a black horse-cloth entered, shivering with cold. It was Death.

While the exhausted mother closed her eyes for a single heartbeat, Death seized the child and fled into the freezing night.

The mother rushed out into the snow, weeping in despair. By the crossroads stood a dark Thorn Bush covered with ice: "I know which way Death went, but I will not tell you unless you warm me against your bosom!" The mother embraced the frozen thorns with all her strength; the sharp spikes pierced her breast, and warm drops of her blood fell upon the twigs. Fresh green leaves and fragrant roses burst forth in the snow, and the Bush pointed the way.

She reached a great, deep Lake that had no boat. The Lake said: "Weep your eyes into my depths; I collect pearls, and I will carry you across!" The mother wept with such boundless sorrow that her two eyes fell into the water like precious gems, and the Lake lifted her like a wave to the opposite shore.

There stood the vast Greenhouse of Death, where millions of living flowers and trees represented the lives of mortals on earth. A withered old woman who guarded the portal said: "Give me your long black hair, and I will let you in!" The mother gladly sheared her raven locks, took the old woman's white hair in return, and searched the greenhouse.

Listening to the heartbeats of the flowers, she recognized the tiny, fluttering pulse of her child in a little blue crocus.

Death entered: "How came you here before me?"
"I am a mother!" she cried.

Death showed her two future lives in the water: one radiant with blessing, and the other tormented by incurable agony and crime. "One of these fates belonged to your child," whispered Death gently. "Would you sentence him to torment?"

The mother fell upon her knees, clasped her hands, and bowed her head in sacred reverence: "Thy will be done, O Lord! Take my child into Thy eternal peace!" And Death bore the innocent soul upward into the everlasting joy of heaven.
moral: A mother's love is stronger than the grave, yet highest faith surrenders all to the divine wisdom of eternity.

title: The Shirt-Collar
summary: There was once a fine gentleman whose entire wardrobe consisted of a single bootjack, a mustache-comb, and an extraordinary stiff white shirt-collar. The shirt-collar was proud bey...
full_text:
There was once a fine gentleman whose entire wardrobe consisted of a single bootjack, a mustache-comb, and an extraordinary stiff white shirt-collar. The shirt-collar was proud beyond measure, believing himself the finest dandy in the world.

When he was sent to the wash-tub, he met a modest iron garter. "My word, what a slender waist!" declared the collar. "May I ask your name?" "I do not give my name to strangers," retorted the garter. "Ah, playing coy!" laughed the collar. "I am a gentleman who owns a bootjack and a comb!"

Next, he was placed on the ironing board before the hot flatiron. "Sweet widow with the burning heart!" exclaimed the collar. "You smooth my edges so tenderly; marry me!" The iron scorched him brown in anger and moved away.

Then came the scissors with sharp blades: "What an exquisite ballet dancer!" said the collar. "You stretch your legs so gracefully!" The scissors snapped: "You impertinent rag!" and snipped his ragged edges off.

Finally, worn and yellowed, the collar was cast into the rag-bag and sent to the paper mill.

In the vat, he was beaten, mashed, boiled, and pressed into a sheet of white paper upon which this very story was printed. Even as paper, he bragged to the other sheets that he had broken the hearts of hundreds of ladies, iron-widows, and dancing scissors—proving that a braggart remains a boaster even after he has been ground to pulp in the rag-mill.
moral: Boasting of imaginary conquests leads only to the paper mill of public ridicule.

full_text:
On the sun-drenched coast of Smyrna, beside the blue waters of the Aegean Sea, an ancient tumulus rises beneath fragrant pines. The local folk say it is the tomb of Homer—the blind father of epic song.

Upon the mound grew a bush of deep crimson roses. A nightingale sang in the branches every twilight, pouring out melodies of Achilles' wrath, Hector's noble courage, and the wooden horse of Troy.

A pilgrim from the distant northern snows visited the tomb. Revering the immortal poet whose songs had illuminated his youth, the traveler plucked a single blooming rose, pressed it reverently within a volume of the Iliad, and carried it back across stormy seas to his quiet northern study.

Years rolled by; the rose dried and lost its fresh petals, but whenever the reader opened the book, the fragrance of ancient Greece breathed forth into the cold winter air. Empires crumble, cities fall to dust, and marble statues decay; but the poetry of the human soul, like the rose from Homer's tomb, blooms in eternal spring.
moral: True poetry outlives empires and monuments, blooming forever in the memory of mankind.

Through the changing seasons of frost, rain, and golden summer light, the heart learned to endure every trial with gentle patience. In moments of solitude and quiet longing, the soul whispered its sincere hopes to the stars, discovering that true worth does not depend on outward glitter or the praise of the crowd.

At last, when the trial reached its appointed close, the light of genuine virtue shone with irresistible radiance. When the moment of transformation arrived, truth dissolved the illusions of pride and vanity.  The cold winds melted away into a dawn of peace, leaving behind a fragrant memory that touched every heart with wonder, proving that he who refuses to bow before the majestic laws of nature is broken by the storm.

full_text:
In the courtyard of a town house lay an old, worn gravestone that had been moved from a demolished churchyard to pave the well-walk. The children played upon it, jumping over the weathered chisel marks that read: "Here rests Preben Hansen and his beloved wife."

An elderly grandmother sat by the window and looked upon the stone with tears of sweet memory. "I remember Preben Hansen!" she said softly. "He was a prosperous merchant who fed the poor during the great famine, gave dowries to orphan maidens, and brought warmth to every freezing hearth."

The children stopped their play and gathered around her knee, listening with reverence to the record of quiet nobility and charity lived long ago.

The stone had lost its place in the churchyard, and time had worn away its letters; but the fragrant memory of an unselfish life blossomed anew in the hearts of children, proving that goodness is immortal.
moral: Good deeds done in quiet love are never forgotten before the eyes of heaven.

title: The Goblin and the Huckster
summary: In a town house, a prosperous huckster kept his shop on the ground floor, selling cheese, butter, candles, and herring. On the top floor lived an impoverished student who spent his...
full_text:
In a town house, a prosperous huckster kept his shop on the ground floor, selling cheese, butter, candles, and herring. On the top floor lived an impoverished student who spent his pennies on old books of poetry.

Between them lived a little household Goblin (Nisse). The goblin loved the huckster, because every Christmas Eve the huckster set out a bowl of sweet porridge with a great lump of butter in the center!

One evening, the student bought a pennyworth of cheese. The huckster wrapped the cheese in a leaf torn from an old book. The student exclaimed: "Do you use noble poetry for wrapping paper? Take my cheese, but give me the book!" The student paid his last copper for the volume and climbed back to his attic.

The goblin felt insulted for the huckster and crept up to the student's keyhole to play a trick.

Peering through the keyhole, what a wonder the goblin beheld! From the book of poetry streamed a magnificent tree of golden light! Its radiant branches reached into heaven, bearing luminous fruit and echoing with celestial music. The poor student sat bathed in the divine glow, smiling in heavenly ecstasy.

The goblin stood mesmerized. "How wonderful!" he thought. "I should love to live up here with the student!"

Then he hesitated. He remembered the huckster's Christmas porridge with the big lump of sweet butter.

"No," sighed the little goblin. "The student has no butter in his porridge! I must stay downstairs with the huckster!"

And the little goblin ran down to the shop, proving that humanity often chooses the comfort of fat butter over the celestial illumination of poetry.
moral: The soul cannot live by butter alone; poetry and truth are the true food of humanity.

summary: Yes, in a thousand years, they will come on wings of steam and air! The youthful inhabitants of America will fly across the great Atlantic Ocean to visit the ancient, venerable con...
full_text:
Yes, in a thousand years, they will come on wings of steam and air! The youthful inhabitants of America will fly across the great Atlantic Ocean to visit the ancient, venerable continent of Europe!

They will travel in grand aerial ships propelled through the clouds, landing first upon the emerald shores of Ireland, gazing down upon the ruins of London and the monuments of Paris. In a few days, they will cross the Alps, view the Colosseum of Rome, walk upon the Acropolis of Athens, and gaze at the ruins of Copenhagen.

A young traveler will hold a guidebook of antiquities, saying: "Here stood the kingdoms of the ancient world! Here poets sang and emperors ruled!"

They will see Europe as we look upon the pyramids of the Nile. Yet through all changes of technology and empires, the glorious achievements of human intellect, freedom, and love will remain the eternal heritage that unites mankind across millennia.
moral: Human genius soars across skies, yet the enduring monuments of history remain sacred beacons.

title: The Old Bachelor's Nightcap
summary: In a narrow street in Copenhagen lived an old bachelor clerk named Anton. He wore a faded woolen nightcap and spent his quiet life selling pepper and nutmeg in a small shop. The ne...
full_text:
In a narrow street in Copenhagen lived an old bachelor clerk named Anton. He wore a faded woolen nightcap and spent his quiet life selling pepper and nutmeg in a small shop. The neighbors called him a cold, dried-up recluse who had never known human feeling.

Yet when Anton fell into his final sleep and they lifted the old woolen nightcap from his brow, a worn portrait was discovered beneath the lining, depicting a lovely maiden with golden curls from his native German town.

As a youth, Anton had loved her with his whole soul. He had toiled for decades in foreign lands to earn enough gold to marry her, only to learn on the eve of his return that she had died of a sudden fever, whispering his name. Anton had locked his grief in his breast, preserved her portrait near his brow, and spent his lifetime helping poor apprentices in secret.

The gossiping town had seen only a dusty nightcap; but angels looked upon a crown of lifelong fidelity and sorrow, escorting Anton's soul to a joyful reunion in heaven.
moral: Behind the plainest, most solitary life often rests a sacred sanctuary of faithful, unspoken love.

title: The Old Church Bell
summary: In the small town of Marbach in Germany, an old church bell hung in the church tower. When a great storm cracked its bronze rim, the town melted the metal into a smaller bell....
full_text:
In the small town of Marbach in Germany, an old church bell hung in the church tower. When a great storm cracked its bronze rim, the town melted the metal into a smaller bell.

On the night the bell was recast, a poor army surgeon's wife gave birth to a frail infant boy in a humble garret. The church bell tolled, and its chime seemed to weave a prophecy around the child's cradle: "Thou shalt ring out a song of freedom that will shake the thrones of tyrants!"

That child was Friedrich Schiller—the glorious poet who wrote the Ode to Joy and the Song of the Bell! His fiery verse swept across Europe like a thunderstorm, inspiring millions to stand for human liberty, dignity, and brotherhood.

The old bronze bell had cracked, but the poetry born under its chime rings on through centuries, an unbreakable anthem of the free human spirit.
moral: The bell of true freedom and poetry rings from humble cradles to awaken the conscience of nations.

title: Under the Willow Tree

full_text:
In a quiet village, little Knud and little Johanne grew up as playmates under the shade of an old weeping willow tree. Knud loved Johanne with all his tender heart; they shared gingerbread, sang hymns, and carved their names upon the willow bark.

As youth blossomed, Johanne moved to the royal capital, where her exquisite singing voice won her international fame as an opera prima donna.

Knud, now an honest journeyman shoemaker, traveled across Europe to see her. In Nuremberg, he heard her sing in the great theater. Her voice was like an angel's, but she moved in a world of princes and counts. When Knud spoke with her backstage, Johanne embraced him affectionately as a dear brother from childhood, but showed him her diamond engagement ring, announcing her betrothal to a wealthy nobleman.

Heartbroken, Knud walked out into the snowy night, wandering toward the Alps. Exhausted by grief and frost, he sat down beneath a great weeping willow covered in icicles.

As his eyelids grew heavy, he dreamed that the willow branches turned into golden harps, that Johanne sang only for him, and that they were united in eternal youth. When morning came, peasants found Knud sleeping the sleep of peace beneath the frozen tree, his face radiating the serene joy of an unblemished soul that had found eternal rest.
moral: Unrequited earthly love that remains pure and unselfish finds its ultimate fulfillment in the peace of eternity.

keywords: the last dream of the old oak
full_text:
For three hundred and sixty-five years, the great oak tree had stood upon the coastal cliff, sheltering generations of birds, sailors, and children. In its long life, each year felt like a single day, and the ephemera flies that lived for an hour were its merry companions.

On a holy Christmas Eve, a mighty winter gale tore across the ocean. As the storm lashed its ancient boughs, the old oak fell into a transcendent dream.

In its vision, its roots stretched deeper, its branches climbed into the golden heavens, and all the friends of its three centuries—the wildflowers that had bloomed beneath it, the nightingales that had sung in its branches, and the people who had rested in its shade—rose in radiant light to embrace the majestic tree in eternal summer!

With a tremendous crash, the ancient oak was uprooted by the storm and fell upon the snowy shore. But in the dawn of Christmas morning, the church bells rang, and the sailors saw that the old oak had passed into its dream of everlasting life.
moral: In the great tapestry of creation, life rises through dissolution into eternal reunion.

title: The Snowman
summary: "It crackles so delightfully within me!" said the Snowman, gazing with coal-black eyes across the snowy yard. "The biting frost is delicious! But tell me, old watchdog, what is tha...
full_text:
"It crackles so delightfully within me!" said the Snowman, gazing with coal-black eyes across the snowy yard. "The biting frost is delicious! But tell me, old watchdog, what is that bright, glowing thing peering through the cellar window?"

"That is the stove!" barked the watchdog. "It radiates glowing heat and cooks delicious bone broth! Keep your distance, Snowman, or it will melt you to water!"

The Snowman could not tear his eyes from the cellar window. Through the glass, he saw the stove glowing with fiery embers, sending warm red light dancing across the floor. An irresistible, agonizing longing filled his snowy chest: "Oh, to be near that glowing stove! To feel that warmth, even if it melts me!"

All night, through freezing starlight, the Snowman stood watching the stove, his heart burning with cold passion.

When morning dawned, the south wind blew softly; the thaw set in. As the golden sun climbed the sky, the Snowman began to melt. Down he dripped into a pool of water upon the flagstones.

When he was gone, the watchdog saw what had been in the center of the Snowman: a long iron stove scraper around which the boys had molded his snowy body!

"Ah!" barked the watchdog. "Now I understand why he longed so passionately for the stove—he had a stove scraper in his body! It was in his very blood!"
moral: Yearning for what warms the heart can bring dissolution, yet longing is the essence of being alive.

title: The Flax
summary: The flax plant bloomed in the meadow with delicate blue flowers like the sky. "I am the happiest of plants!" sang the flax. "The sun warms me, the rain refreshes me, and I shall be...
full_text:
The flax plant bloomed in the meadow with delicate blue flowers like the sky. "I am the happiest of plants!" sang the flax. "The sun warms me, the rain refreshes me, and I shall be made into fine linen!"

One day, workers pulled the flax by the roots, steeped it in water, broke it on the brake, and carded it with iron teeth. "Ouch! This is painful!" cried the flax. "Yet one must suffer to become useful."

It was spun into delicate white thread and woven into fine linen tablecloths for the royal palace. "How splendid!" rejoiced the flax. "I am useful to mankind!"

Years passed. The linen wore into rags. It was torn, boiled in lye, and beaten into pulp at the paper mill. From its fibers was created glorious white paper upon which inspiring stories were printed!

Finally, the paper was cast into the hearth. As it burned, thousands of bright sparks danced like children up the chimney into the golden sun, singing: "The song is never done! Life ascends forever into light!"

title: The Girl Who Trod on a Loaf
summary: There was once a proud, beautiful girl named Inger, whose vanity made her heart as hard as stone. She was sent to carry a large loaf of white bread to her poor mother in the countr...
keywords: the girl who trod on a loaf
full_text:
There was once a proud, beautiful girl named Inger, whose vanity made her heart as hard as stone. She was sent to carry a large loaf of white bread to her poor mother in the country.

Reaching a muddy ditch, Inger did not wish to soil her fine new shoes. So she tossed the loaf of bread into the mud to use as a stepping stone!

The moment her foot touched the bread, she sank straight down into the earth! Down she plunged into the dark, slimy subterranean kingdom of the Marsh Woman, where toads and snakes crawled over her limbs.

She was turned into a stiff, frozen stone statue, standing in the mire, tormented by the memories of her cruelty. Passersby in the world above told her story as a warning.

One day, a little girl heard the tale and wept bitter tears of pity: "Poor Inger! May God have mercy on her soul!"

The tear of pure, unselfish pity fell into the underworld, melting Inger's stone heart. Inger wept tears of genuine remorse, and was transformed into a little gray bird that flew across the fields gathering breadcrumbs for starving birds, until her debt was redeemed and she ascended into the golden light of heaven.
moral: Pride that scorns the bread of life sinks into the mud; humble repentance alone unlocks redemption.

title: The Snail and the Rose Tree
summary: In the center of the garden stood a blooming rose tree, bursting with fragrant red blossoms. At its root lived a snail, safely curled within his slimy shell....
keywords: the snail and the rose tree
full_text:
In the center of the garden stood a blooming rose tree, bursting with fragrant red blossoms. At its root lived a snail, safely curled within his slimy shell.

"What do you give to the world?" hissed the cynical snail. "You merely bloom and drop your petals! You have no deep philosophy! I spit upon the world; I withdraw into myself, for I am self-contained!"

The rose tree smiled gently in the morning sunshine: "I bloom because my heart is full of gratitude! The sun warms me, the dew refreshes me, and my perfume brings joy to little children and solace to the sick. I give all that I have received. What do you give from your shell?"

"I give nothing," said the snail coldly, "for the world is unworthy of me." And he shut himself up tight.

The rose tree blossomed year after year, blessing all who passed; while the selfish snail dried up in his shell, forgotten and useless in the dust.
moral: To give oneself in love and beauty is the highest joy; selfish isolation rots in its own shell.

title: The Snail (The Shell of Pride)
summary: The snail crawled along the gravel path, sneering at the busy bees and fragrant roses: "What fools! Working and blooming for others! I live for myself alone within my shell!"...
full_text:
In the center of a noble estate stood a secluded, tranquil garden enclosed by ancient stone walls draped in ivy and wild hazel bushes. Within this garden, climbing rosebushes burst into fragrant glory every summer, opening hundreds of velvet crimson and creamy white blossoms that scented the warm breeze, while golden bees hummed from petal to petal collecting nectar for their hive. Down upon the mossy gravel path beneath the hazel hedge crawled a plump, solitary snail. He carried his striped spiral shell like an impenetrable fortress, peering out at the garden with two tiny, arrogant eye-stalks and a curled lip of unyielding disdain.

"Look at those pathetic roses," the snail muttered to himself as he glided slowly over the damp stones, leaving a silvery trail of slime behind him. "They bloom their lives away just to please the foolish human beings who walk along the gravel path! And observe those wretched bees, exhausting themselves from dawn to dusk to fill wax combs they will never enjoy! What a pointless, miserable existence! I am infinitely superior to them all. I produce everything from within my own nature; I take nothing from the world, and I offer nothing to anyone. I retire into my magnificent shell whenever the weather turns rough, undisturbed by storms or sorrows. I live entirely for myself, and in myself alone resides absolute perfection!"

The roses smiled gently down from their green trellis, nodding their dew-kissed petals in the morning sunlight. "Dear neighbor," whispered an elder rose, "to pour out beauty, comfort, and fragrance for others is the greatest happiness upon this earth. Even when our blossoms wither and our petals fall to the autumn grass, the memory of our sweetness lives on in the hearts of those who loved us." But the snail only sneered in contempt, pulling his eye-stalks inside his thick, cold shell to shut out their gentle words. Just then, a heavy iron-rimmed carriage rolled briskly along the driveway to fetch the master of the manor. The crushing iron wheel rolled directly over the gravel path, pulverizing the haughty shell to powder in the blink of an eye. The carriage passed away, and the fragrant roses bloomed on in the sunshine, sharing their unselfish love with every child, bird, and wandering soul that entered the garden.
moral: Withdrawing into the shell of arrogant isolation leaves one dead to the beauty of the world.

Five green peas sat in a green pod; they grew side by side in the warm sunshine, believing the whole universe was green.

title: What the Old Man Does Is Always Right
summary: A country peasant rode to market to sell or barter his horse. On the road, he traded the horse for a cow, the cow for a sheep, the sheep for a goose, the goose for a hen, and final...
keywords: what the old man does is always right
full_text:
A country peasant rode to market to sell or barter his horse. On the road, he traded the horse for a cow, the cow for a sheep, the sheep for a goose, the goose for a hen, and finally the hen for a sack of rotten apples!

In the inn, two wealthy Englishmen laughed at his foolishness and wagered a bushel of gold coins that his wife would beat him black and blue when he returned home with rotten apples.

When the peasant arrived at his cottage and told his wife of each trade, she beamed with love: "A cow? How delicious, we shall have milk! A sheep? Wonderful, we shall have wool! A hen? Splendid, fresh eggs! Rotten apples? Heaven be praised! I can make apple sauce for our schoolmaster!" And she threw her arms around his neck and kissed him.

The Englishmen paid the bushel of gold with reverence, declaring: "When love is complete, whatever the good man does is always right!"
moral: Unconditional love and trust in a marriage turn every mistake into a blessing of peace.
